English: When Li Zongren, Bai Chongxi, and Chen Jitang read their 'Anti-Japanese declaration' and formed a joint 'National Revolutionary Anti-Japanese National Salvation Army', they expected other warlords and even the Communists to join their cause and help them put an end to Chiang. This proved to be a miscalculation, as most other warlords were weakened and weary of confronting Chiang after the failed attempt in 1930, and even the Communists were opposed to the idea. The last attempt to displace Chiang in 1930 caused a civil war, hundreds of thousands of casualties, weakened China, and enabled the Japanese to conquer Manchuria. The last thing that USSR wanted was to enable the Japanese to conquer even more territory, so the word from Moscow was strongly negative. Instead, just as Guandong's army started its advance into Hunan, dissention quickly developed within the ranks of the plotters. At the cost of a few concessions, appeasement of the plotters, and monetary rewards, Chiang was able to sway much of the Guandong clique to turn against Chen Jitang. Even Chen's Chief of staff Lee Han-hoon was swayed by Chiang Kai-shek, and fled to Hong Kong, making it clear that he did not intend to stand on the side of Chen Jitang.

English: In 1934, the USSR intervened in Xinjiang on behalf of the local warlord Sheng Shicai and helped him establish control over much of the province, but the Soviet troops did not advance beyond Turfan, partly out of fear of Chinese and international backlash, and fear of a potentially costly occupation as well. The fighting died down in 1935, with Xinjiang divided in two and the Uyghur rebels playing as the third force and staging occasional uprisings against both sides. In 1937, another major Uyghur uprising broke out and caused resumption of fighting, with the Uyghur this time tactically allied with the pro-KMT forces. The Soviets once again intervened to help their ally and inflicted a strategic defeat on the pro-KMT and Uyghur rebels, forcing them to withdraw from the province entirely.

Likewise, Xinjiang would have to be de-facto abandoned to the Soviets, although it would nominally remain a part of China.

English: As the tide of war turned with the Communist victory in Manchuria, Chiang concluded in late 1948 that he needed to move to Taiwan; by end 1948 he had started shipments of China's important cultural artefacts and financial reserves to Taiwan. By 1948–1949, most of the northern mainland fell to the communists after the three decisive campaigns of Liaoshen, Pingjin and Huaihai. In mid-April 1949, the Chinese Red Army — now called the People's Liberation Army — crossed the Yangtze River and captured the Nationalist capital Nanjing and the major city of Shanghai, later Guangzhou, followed by Chongqing and then Chengdu. Mao proclaimed the establishment of a new republic in Beijing on October 1, while Chiang fled to the island of Formosa (Taiwan), where approximately 300,000 soldiers had already been airlifted.

English: With the imminent fall of the Nationalist government, the many former warlords were quick to pledge allegiance to the new rulers of China. Tibet, however, was a somewhat different story. Like Mongolia, Tibet had declared its independence from China after the revolution of 1912 overthrew the Qing dynasty. Ever since then, the Tibetan government under the Dalai Lamas maintained local autonomy in one form or another, however, its independence has not been regocnized by any other power - save for Mongolia. In addition, there was an unresolved conflict over the border of Tibet, which led to frequent clashes against various Chinese governments and factions. When the Communist armies approached Tibet, the 10th Dalai Lama sent representatives to Beijing to open negotiations for the peaceful incorporation of Tibet into China. The negotiations proceeded in a somewhat tense atmosphere and while the Chinese and Tibetan armies were clashing over the disputed territories. However, Dalai Lama recognized that Tibet's ability to assert independence from the PLA was ultimately futile, and in the end, he consented to the so-called 'Seventeen Point Agreement', which affirmed Chinese sovereignty over Tibet on the condition of the preservation of Tibet's vast autonomy. This vast autonomy, including its separate political structure, economic system, and even armed forces, remained in force until the Tibetan uprising of 1959, after which Tibet was properly annexed into the People's Republic of China.

English: After having been nearly extinguished in 1936, the Chinese Communist Party began to gradually recover, using both the Long March and the resistance against Japan as effective propaganda tools. Their fortunes grew even brighter with the outbreak of full-scale war against Japan in 1937. For the most part, the CCP-affiliated units tried to avoid engaging in frontal battles against the Japanese and concentrated on guerilla warfare, which proved to be highly effective not only at disrupting the Japanese and their collaborators, but equally so at spreading the appeal of Communism in the Japanese-occupied territory as a natural antagonist to the reactionary Japanese ideology. The communists aggressively expanded their influence within the occupied territories by various means, from spreading Marxist propaganda to harassing rival rebel groups into submission. From the humble start of less than 100,000 foot soldiers in 1936, the Communist armies grew steadily over the course of the war, such that by 1945 they had more than 1.3 million men under arms, with a separate militia of over 2.6 million.

The CCP leadership, for its part, has grown confident of its increased strength, and wanted to put it to good use and show it off to the world, establishing itself as a major anti-Japanese fighting force. The offensive was a qualified success. While many of its initial gains were eventually reversed, the Japanese were humiliated and their plans were disrupted. As a side effect, Chiang grew even more weary and frightened of the CCP's growing strength.

In a short time, the Japanese army mobilized tens of thousands of troops to launch retaliatory 'sweep' operations across the anti-Japanese base areas in North China. These operations were marked by the brutal implementation of the 'Three Alls Policy' - burn all, kill all, loot all. In response, the Eighth Route Army had to shift back to defensive counter-sweep operations, relying on mobile guerrilla tactics to wear down the enemy forces, and the offensive was effectively over.

English: A few months prior to the incident, KMT military leadership escalated its criticisms of the CCP military strategy. Chiang accused CCP's Fourth Army in particular of establishing partisan bases in the Nanjing region, in Anhui and Jiangsu, and in doing so, violating the balance of power in China and defying the orders of the Military Commission regarding troop dispositions. During a heated argument with Zhou Enlai, Chiang declared that the CCP 'showed itself to be dishonorable, moved to another region, expanded its influence, increased its troops without permission, organized partisan detachments, and concentrated its troops around the troops of the central government.' To settle the issue, Chiang categorically demanded that CCP withdraw its forces north of Yellow River within a month. Under intense pressure, the CCP agreed to move its troops north of the Yangtze River, and regiments of the 4th Army under Ye Ting started to move towards Jiangsu, planning to cross the river along three routes. However, Chiang's frustration had already reached a boiling point, and he ordered the Communists to be surrounded and destroyed by an overwhelming force during their attempt to cross. After days of fighting, the 9000 strong Communit force was practically destroyed by the overwhelming numbers of Nationalist troops. Ye Ting, wanting to save his men, went to the KMT headquarters to negotiate terms, but he was detained upon arrival and threatened with execution. The incident led to effective breakdown of the United Front between CCP and KMT. Intense foreign pressure by both USSR and the US barely managed to avoid further escalation, but any further cooperation between CCP and KMT from that point was brought to a minimum. The incident also led to the winding down of Soviet aid to China and its gradual replacement with American aid.

English: Despite a breakdown of cooperation between KMT and CCP, when the Japanese forces invaded the CCP base area in Yan'an, Chiang Kai-Shek came under immense pressure to assist them, or at least - to allow their evacuation. After all, officially we are both still part of the National Revolutionary Army, and part of the anti-Japanese united front. Despite a tempting situation, facilitating the destruction of the CCP forces by Japan was hardly acceptable option from a policial standpoint, not to mention, it could make continued struggle against Japan a lot more challenging. Facing a difficult situation, the CCP also reached out and promised obedience in return for reconciliation. But do we trust them?

English: One of Mao's chief reasons for choosing Yan'an as the place to set up a new base of operations was its proximity to the Japanese occupied territory and the possiblity of engaging in battle against the Japanese. Aside from Mao's sincere belief that Japan was a growing danger to China which had to be confronted, he was also hoping to use the struggle against Japan as a way to boost the CCP's popularity and undermine the morale of the troops sent by KMT to destroy it. His prediction proved to be correct - with the anti-Japanese feelings running rampant everywhere from the National Army to the peasantry, every move the CCP made directed against Japan hugely boosted its popularity and contrasted favorably with the passive appeasement policy followed by KMT. So much so, that many warlord units nominally under the KMT control flat out refused to fight the Communists. But to stay true to this path, the Communists had to make a bold move which would prove that their desire to confront Japan is sincere, and not just an empty propaganda ploy. To do this, in February 1936, Communist leaders Xu Haidong and Liu Zhidan led 34,000 Communist guerillas into southwestern Shanxi, which was ruled by a Nationalist-aligned warlord, Yan Xishan, and demanded that he let them through his territory so that they can reach Chahar, where the Anti-Japanese volunteer armies were being hard-pressed by Japan. This was a massive gamble, but the CCP calculated that the material risks of the operation were far outweighed by the potential political gains.

English: The Korean People's Revolutionary Army was established on 25 April 1932 as a guerilla force operating against the Japanese and their allies largely in Manchuria in alliance with the local Chinese resistance. In 1935, the CCP's delegation to Comintern issued a letter to the party organization in Manchuria, which called for the implementation of the all-out Counter-Japanese united front, regardless of party, class, or ethnicity. This officially created the Northeast Counter-Japanese United Army, of which KPRA was a constituent part. Kim Il Sung, later to become the leader of North Korea, was a high-ranking officer in this army, and attained a distinction where he crossed the Manchurian-Korean border and attacked a Japanese police station in Pochonbo at 1937. This event was widely reported by Korean newspapers such as Donga Ilbo and he became famous in Korea as the most prominent leader of the Counter-Japanese movement in the northern half.

English: The tattered remnants of the Northeast Counter-Japanese United Army had escaped to the USSR but continued launching small cross-border raids for some time, which achieved very little but kept Japan on its toes. In 1941, the USSR signed a non-aggresion treaty with Japan, and the cross-border raids had to cease. In 1942 the USSR officially disbanded the NCJUA, and out of its remnants it formed the 88th Separate Rifle Brigade of the Soviet Army. The Brigade was stationed in the Far East and did not see combat on the German front, but in 1945 it finally saw action during the Soviet invasion of Manchuria. After the end of the operation, the unit was disbanded and its veterans went on to join the Chinese Red Army and the Korean People's Army. Among the Korean members of the NCJUA was Kim Il Sung, the future leader of North Korea.

English: With the war in a state of stalemate and Japan distracted by struggle for the Pacific, the CCP was experiencing a time of relative peace when they could focus on internal affairs. Mao decided to use this precious time to undertake significant internal reform and consolidation of the Party, which was growing rapidly due to the influx of new recruites from the Nationalist and occupied areas. The main aims of the reform were to adjust the party ideology from the Moscow dogma closer to the Chinese conditions, thus improving strategy and broadening its appeal; to consolidate the new and existing members ideologically and instill discipline and unity in party ranks; and last but not least - to purge influential rivals from the party who may pose a challenge to Mao's personal authority, and may sabotage the unity of the overall movement at a critical moment. While temporarily disrputive and divisive, the movement is overall credited as a long term success and its legacy proved fundamental to the subsequent history of the Chinese Communist Party.

English: After the defeat of France in 1940, the Free French Forces were formed to continue the fight against Germany. The initial strength of this force was just 1,300 men from the Expeditionary Force in Norway and the French Legion, plus a few African garrisons which chose to side with de Gaulle. Over the course of the next few years, this force gradually grew to 80,000 men, bolstered by Vichy defectors and Frenchmen fleeing from the occupied territories. It ceased to exist in January 1943 when it was merged with the much larger French Army of Africa, which defected in whole from the Vichy government, and formed a new structure called French Liberation Army.

English: Seven hours before the expiration of the Japanese ultimatum, Martin and Nishihara signed an agreement authorizing the stationing of 6,000 Japanese troops in Tonkin north of the Red River, the use of four airfields in Tonkin, the right to move up to 25,000 troops through Tonkin to Yunnan and the right to move one division of the Twenty-Second Army through Tonkin via Haiphong for use elsewhere in China. The accord had been communicated to all relevant commands by 21:00, an hour before the ultimatum was set to expire. The Twenty-Second Army, however, did not intend to wait to take advantage of the accord. Lieutenant-General Aketo Nakamura, commander of the 5th Infantry Division, sent columns across the border near Dong Dang at precisely 22:00. At Dong Dang there was an exchange of fire that quickly spread to other border posts overnight. The French position at the railhead at Lang Son was surrounded by Japanese armour and forced to surrender after days of fighting. Meanwhile, Japanese aircraft from aircraft carriers in the Gulf of Tonkin attacked French positions on the coast. The French Government protested the breach of the agreements by the IJA to the Japanese governmentm and a French Government envoy came to negotiate
French: in the meantime, shore defenses remained under orders to open fire on any attempted landing. On 26 September, Japanese forces came ashore at Dong Tac, south of Haiphong, and moved on the port. A second landing put tanks ashore, and Japanese planes bombed Haiphong, causing some casualties. By early afternoon the Japanese force of some 4,500 troops and a dozen tanks were outside Haiphong. By the evening of 26 September, fighting had died down. Japan took possession of Gia Lam Airbase outside Hanoi, the rail marshaling yard on the Yunnan border at Lao Cai, and Phu Lang Thuong on the railway from Hanoi to Lang Son, and stationed 900 troops in the port of Haiphong and 600 more in Hanoi.

English: In early 1941, the situation in East Asia changed dramatically. Japan was able to work out a non-aggression deal with the USSR which led to the winding down of Soviet aid to China, while at the same time, the US began to take an increasingly active role in assisting China and sabotaging Japan by every possible means. It is in this atmosphere that Japan was able to persuade France to sign a protocol 'Concerning Joint Defense and Joint Military Cooperation' with Japan. This agreement defined the Franco-Japanese relationship for Indochina. It gave the Japanese a total of eight airfields, allowed them to have more troops present, and to use the Indochinese financial system, in return for a fragile French autonomy. Some 140,000 Japanese troops thus landed in southern French Indochina on 28 July 1941.

Some 140,000 Japanese troops thus landed in southern French Indochina on 28 July 1941.

The first attack was meant as more of a warning, and the majority of the bombs were deliberately dropped short of their target. But the raids continued, especially once the British attempted to help the rogue general De Gaulle wrestle control over the French colony of Senegal. The battle of Dakar was a failure for the Allies, with several British ships receiving heavy damage, and further Vichy raids on Gibraltar followed suit. 64 French bombers took off from Morocco and dropped 150 bombs on Gibraltar, dealing heavy damage to the fort and naval base, as well as several auxillary ships. The next day, the French returned with another bombing raid. However, as the Allies withdrew from Dakar, the French ceased their bombing raids and the tensions cooled once again.

English: Following the successful Allied landings in North Africa, Vichy French generals folded under pressure and decided to switch sides. Francois Darlan had persuaded the Army of Africa to switch over to the Allies, however he was a very contraversial figure, and he was assasinated by an anti-Vichy monarchist just two months later. General Henri Giraud, considered somewhat less contraversial among the Allies, assumed command of the French African troops. The French African Army was then merged together with the Free French Forces under de Gaulle into a single structure, the French Army of Liberation. Effectively, the remnants of the Vichy forces were now part of the liberation movement.

English: As part of the deal with the Allies, Francois Darlan, formerly Prime Minister under Petain, remained in charge of French North Africa. This effectively created two parallel French governments and military formations under Allied control. Following his assassination in December 1942, Darlan was replaced by General Henri Giraud, but the division remained. De Gaulle distrusted and fiercely opposed Giraud, calling for a purge and non-recognition of the former Vichy collaborators. Nonetheless, under Allied pressure, the different branches of Free France, led by de Gaulle out of London and Giraud out of Algeria, were finally merged into one, creating the unified French Committee of National Liberation, initially under joint leadership of Giraud and De Gaulle.

English: Although overall defensive in nature, the Allied plan for dealing with a likely German assault through the low countries involved a rapid deployment of significant French and allied forces to Belgium in the event of an attack. The so-called 'Plan D' envisioned approximately 20 French and 10 British divisions entering Belgium and setting up defenses along the Dyle river. This was partly intended to prevent the German forces from reaching French soil, particularly key industrial areas in the north, but the plan also had a political dimension. Failure to render assistance to the Belgian (and possibly Dutch) forces resisting a German invasion would be seen as cowardice and betrayal, and it would likely result either to the rapid destruction or rapid surrender of their forces, and a political fallout at home. To prevent this, we must deploy no less than 30 divisions to Belgium within a week from today and save it from being overrun until at least that point.

Meanwhile, the Belgian army quickly capitulated, and its captured officers loudly accused the Allies of treason - with their testimonies eagerly broadcast by the German propaganda.

English: When Operation Barbarossa began, the Soviet authorities declared their representatives of Vichy France persona non grata and asked them to return to France. Colonel Charles Luguet, the air attache of the Vichy government in Moscow, changed his allegiance to Free French. De Gaulle, believing in the importance of French soldiers serving on all fronts of the war, decided to engage forces on the Eastern Front in 1942. He initially proposed to send a mechanized division (the future 1st Free French Division, under General Edgard de Larminat) to the Eastern front. British opposition and the advice of Free French Air Forces commander Martial Henri Valin, however, made him opt for an air unit instead. Negotiations were lengthy, and Colonel Pougachev (military chief of the mission in London) opposed a separate French group near the Red Army.

English: The Fezzan campaign was a series of military operations conducted from late 1941 to early 1943 by Free French forces based in Chad, supported by the British Long Range Desert Group, to capture the Fezzan region of Italian Libya. Fezzan, a vast desert province in southwestern Libya bordering French Equatorial Africa, featured strategic oases like Murzuq, Sabha, and Ghat, defended by small Italian garrisons amid challenging arid terrain and limited logistics.\n \nThe campaign began with reconnaissance raids and skirmishes, progressing to the seizure of key settlements, finally linking southern advances with the Allied forces pushing from Egypt and Tunisia. This effort disrupted Axis control over trans-Saharan routes and secured Fezzan under French administration after the war.

English: The 1907 Hague Conventions spelled out a set of standards on naval warfare which were ratified by nearly all sovereign nations, and which became known as 'prize rules' or sometimes 'cruiser rules'. The development of submarines, however, drastically changed the nature of naval warfare, making the application of 'prize rules' very impractical and bordering on impossible. It would require submarines to surface, to stop and inspect merchant ships if suspected of carrying contraband, to protect the crew and passengers, to only sink the ships if crew safety is ensured, and to avoid civilian ships and neutrals engaging in legitimate trade. Germany's failure to adhere to these rules during WW1 was one of the major reasons for the US intervention in that war against Germany. Nevertheless, in 1936, 35 nations - including Germany, have signed the London Submarine Protocol, which confirmed that the 1907 Convention applies to submarines, and pledged to abide by the 'prize rules' regime. As soon as the war began, however, all combatant nations have immediately disregarded this Protocol and proceeded to wage a campaign of unrestricted submarine warfare against each other, leading to frequent naval incidents and large civilian losses. Even the occasional attempts to reign in the submarine warfare for humanitarian reasons instantly fell apart - such as the German attempt to rescue the crew of RMS Laconia.\n\nDespite the circumstances, we can order our submarines and surface vessels to strictly adhere to the rules spelled out in the treaties. This will make our blockade efforts much less effective, but it will also lower our wartime belligerence and potentially help keep neutrals from siding against us.

English: Following the successful occupation of Poland, the representatives of Germany and USSR met again to discuss adjustments to the original Molotov-Ribbentrop treaty. One of the major agreements was a border adjustment which alotted a far greater share of Poland to Germany than originally planned. To compensate, Germany renounced its interests in Lithuania, and the country was transferred to the Soviet sphere of influence. In addition, the treaty stipulated the exchange of Soviet and German nationals between the two occupied zones of Poland and committment by both parties to not allow their territory to be used for any 'Polish agitation' directed at the other party.

Franco initiated negotiations in the spring of 1943 and finally gave the order to withdraw the Azul division in the fall. Some Spanish volunteers refused to return. In the end, the total of 'non-returners' were close to 3,000 men, mostly Falangists. Spaniards also joined other German units, and fresh volunteers slipped across the Spanish border near Lourdes in occupied France. The new pro-German Spanish units were collectively called the Legion Azul ('Blue Legion').

English: The near-simultaneous invasions of Norway by Germany and the Allies for the most part achieved their goals and caught the Norwegian forces off guard. As the Germans occupied Oslo, Norway's former defense miniser Vidkun Quisling entered the broadcasting studios with German backing and proclaimed the formation of a new government with himself as prime minister. His government lacked legitimacy and lasted for only 6 days before the opposition from King Haakon VII, the Norwegian populace, military, and bureaucracy caused it to collapse. Seeing this, Germany also lost interest in Quisling and advised him to resign in favor of a transitional administration which eventually paved way for the German occupation authority.

English: After less than six hours the Danish government surrendered, believing that resistance was futile and hoping to work out an advantageous agreement with Germany. Not only was the flat Jutland territory a perfect area for the German army to operate in, the surprise attack on Copenhagen had made any attempt to defend Zealand impossible. Believing that further resistance would only result in the futile loss of more Danish lives, the Danish cabinet ultimately decided to bow to the German pressure. As a result of the cooperative attitude of the Danish authorities, German officials claimed that they would respect Danish sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as neutrality. They also hoped to score propaganda points by making Denmark, in Hitler's words, 'a model protectorate'. However, the relationship broke down after just a couple of years.

English: When the German infantry arrived at the Amalienborg Palace in the morning of 9 April, they were met with determined opposition from the King's Royal Guard, which repelled the initial attack, suffering three wounded. This gave Christian X and his ministers time to confer with the Danish Army chief General William Wain Prior. As the discussions were ongoing, several formations of German bombers flew over the city dropping leaflets. Faced with the threat of the Luftwaffe bombing the civilian population of Copenhagen, the Danish government capitulated in exchange for retaining political independence in domestic matters.

English: Denmark managed to work out a rather favourable relationship with Nazi Germany. The government remained somewhat intact, and the parliament continued to function more or less as it had before. They were able to maintain much of their former control over domestic policy. The police and judicial system remained in Danish hands, and unlike most occupied countries, King Christian X remained in the country as Danish head of state. The German Reich was formally represented by a Reichsbevollmachtigter ('Reich Plenipotentiary'), i.e. a diplomat accredited to the Sovereign, a post awarded to Cecil von Renthe-Fink, the German ambassador, and then in November 1942 to the lawyer and SS general Werner Best. Meanwhile, Britain responded to the change in Denmark's status by sending a force to occupy Iceland, Greenland, and the Faroe Islands. The Danish presense in Jutland was limited, and in 1942 Germans ordered the remnants of the Danish army to withdraw from Jutland after an incident involving a telegram communication between Hitler and King Christian.

On the same day, the British government sent a message to the Icelandic government, stating that the UK was willing to assist Iceland in maintaining its independence but would require facilities in Iceland to do so. Iceland was invited to join the UK in the war as a belligerent and an ally. Iceland refused the British offer and stalled the negotiations. Britain responded with Operation Fork and Operation Valentine, forcibly occupying undefended Iceland and Faroe Islands against protests of their local governments.

English: Three years after the initial occupation of Denmark, the relationship began to unravel. In October 1942, Hitler transmitted a long, flattering birthday telegram to King Christian. The King replied with a simple 'Giving my best thanks. King Christian' sending the Fuhrer into a state of rage at this deliberate slight. In March 1943, Denmark held an election, in which the overwhelming majority of the voters supported anti-nazi parties. The election, discontent, and a growing feeling of optimism that Germany would soon be defeated led to widespread strikes and civil disturbances in the summer of 1943. The Danish government refused to deal with the situation to the satisfaction of the Germans, who responded with an ultimatum which the government felt unable to accept. The Danish government refused, so on 29 August 1943 the Germans officially dissolved the Danish government and instituted martial law. The Danish cabinet handed in its resignation, but since King Christian never officially accepted it, the government remained functioning de jure until the end of the war.

English: As the tide of war began to turn against Germany and its allies, Joseph Goebbels delivered a fiery speech to a large, carefully selected audience at the Berlin Sportpalast. The speech was the first public admission by the National Socialist leadership that Germany faced serious dangers. Goebbels called for a total war to secure victory over the Allies, and exhorted the German people to continue the war even though it would be long and difficult, because, as he asserted, both Germany's survival and the survival of Western civilisation were at stake. Around the time of this speech, the government began to take first measures that would eventually lead to the all-out mobilisation of the German economy. Hitler, however, did not think the time was yet ripe for the kinds of extreme measures that Goebbels proposed, and wanted to keep things largely as they were for the time being. It took another year of constant military failure, and an assasination attempt on Hitler himself, before the Furher finally came to the conclusion that only a full-out total war effort could turn the tide. This was also a huge personal success for Goebbels, who told his staff that he had achieved 'practically full dictatorial powers' with the new appointment as the Reich Plenipotentiary for Total War.

English: General Tadeusz Bor-Komorowski signed the capitulation of the remaining Polish forces in the German headquarters in the presence of General Erich von dem Bach-Zelewski. According to the capitulation treaty, the Home Army soldiers were to be treated in accordance with the Geneva Convention and the civilian population was to be treated humanely. English: The swift collapse of the army that Reza Shah had spent so much time and effort creating was humiliating. Many Iranian commanders behaved incompetently, others secretly sympathized with the British and sabotaged Iranian resistance. The army generals met in secret to discuss surrender options. When the Shah learned of the generals' actions, he beat armed forces chief General Ahmad Nakhjavan with a cane and physically stripped him of his rank. Nakhjavan was nearly shot by the Shah on the spot, but at the insistence of the Crown Prince, he was sent to prison instead. In response to the Shah's defiance, the Red Army moved to occupy Tehran. Fearing execution by the Communists, many people (especially the wealthy) fled the city. Reza Shah, in a letter handwritten by Foroughi, announced his abdication, as the Soviets entered the city on 17 September. The British wanted to restore the Qajar dynasty to power, but the heir to Ahmad Shah Qajar, Hamid Hassan Mirza, was a British subject who spoke no Persian. Instead (with the help of Foroughi), Crown Prince Mohammad Reza Pahlavi took the oath to become the Shah of Iran.

English: After world war 2, the eleven states of Malaya formed a single British crown colony known as the Malayan Union. Due to opposition from the Malay nationalists, however, the Union was quickly disbanded and replaced by a self-governing Federation of Malaya in 1948, which transformed Malaya into a self-governing Protectorate of United Kingdom, restored the symbolic positions of the rulers of the Malay states and introduced greater restrictions on the attainment of citizenship status. Like the Malayan Union before it, the Federation did not include Singapore, despite its traditional connections with Malaya. Meanwhile, an insurgent group called Malayan National Liberation Army led by the Communist Party of Malaya and composed largely from the remnants of the wartime anti-Japanese resistance, began to wage a low-level insurgency against the Federation, advocating among other things a complete departure of British and Commonwealth troops from the country and equality for all citizens of Malaya. However, British agreement to gradually restore Malayan independence by peaceful means helped to ensure that the support for MNLA remained limited mostly to the Chinese minority, which largely supported the insurgency as it was denied the equal right to vote in elections, had no land rights to speak of, and was very poor on average. The ethnic Malay population supported MLNA in much smaller numbers. The Federation finally attained full sovereignty on 31 August 1957, and the MNLA insurgency ceased shortly afterwards.

The Wehrmacht prepared for a long occupation of Yugoslavia, but as ever more forces were needed on the Eastern Front help was needed in maintaining the occupation of Yugoslavia. While most Serbs were hostile, some were prepared to work with the occupation for the sake of self-preservation and fulfillment of certain shared objectives such as anti-Communism.

English: In 1941, Ante Pavelic agreed to provide troops for the war against the Soviet Union. Negotiations took some time, however, as Germany preferred for the volunteers to serve directly under the authority of the Wehrmacht and Waffen SS, with no affilitation to NDH. This would have ensued direct German control over combat units, reliable command structures, as well as German standards of equipment, discipline, doctrine, and logistics. Eventually, Pavelic was pressured to agree that the troops would be completely under German control, with the only compomise being that they would swear a dual oath to both Hitler and Pavelic and they would wear distinctive Croat insignia. In all other respects, they would be German.

Their alliance with the Partisans quickly fell apart, however, as the two sides bitterly argued over both the goals and means of resistance. Mihailovic soon began to fear Tito's growing strength and popularity, while at the same time coming to the belief that continued war against the Germans would only cause further massacres against civilians which he was not able to prevent. With that in mind, he eventually resolved to cease active resistance, turn on the Partisans, and seek contact with the German administration in order to find a modus vivendi. He spearheaded a number of agreements between the Chetniks and the Axis powers, establishing the Chetnik movement as de-facto ally of the Axis, although the ultimate goals of the Chetnik movement remained far removed from those of the occupying powers. As a result of these actions, the Chetniks lost recognition and support of the Allied powers, who redirected their aid to Tito's Partisans instead.

English: Since 1923, the Turkish straits have been subject to the Treaty of Lausanne which demilitarised and opened the Straits to unrestricted civilian and military traffic under the supervision of the International Straits Commission of the League of Nations. Turkey was not satisfied with the terms, however, and so were several other nations, and so in April 1935, the Turkish government dispatched a lengthy diplomatic note to the signatories of the Treaty of Lausanne proposing a conference to agree a new regime for the Straits and requested that the League of Nations authorise the reconstruction of the Dardanelles forts. The response to the note was generally favourable, and in July 1936, 10 nations including the key interested parties such as UK and USSR have put their signatures on a new document which would last for decades. This document, among other things, significantly strengthened Turkish control of the straits, also giving Turkey the right to regulate and levy fees on ships passing through these strategic waterways, boosting its revenue from maritime traffic. For France and even more so for Britain, their accession to the treaty was a major concession to Turkey, which they felt obliged to make in order to prevent Turkey from joining the Axis.

The Straits were briefly demilitarized and opened to all foreign traffic as a result of the Ottoman Empire's defeat in World War 1, but after the Montreux Convention of 1936, direct control over the straits again became a matter of both strategic and economic significance. The controller of the straits is authorized to regulate and levy fees on the maritime traffic, and the increased leverage over the regional trade by gives the controller greater bargaining power.

English: Aside from the Armed Forces, most countries also have a separate paramilitary institution called the Gendarmerie, also often referred to as the Internal Troops, or most commonly - the National Guard. The Gendarmerie is typically not a part of the Armed Forces, it has its own chain of command, and it is ultimately subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior rather than the Ministry of Defense. While it is more lightly equipped than the Army, it can often be as numerous or even more numerous than the Army itself. The primary role of the Gendarmerie is to provide internal security, however, it has a role in war as well. While it is not commonly used in offensive operations against the enemy abroad, the Gendarmerie will fight defensively alongside the army should our country become the target of an invasion, and it will provide a sizable boost to the nation's defensive capabilities. The Gendarmerie can also be deployed outside the country to act as a form of military police on the occupied territories as well. Finally, the Gendarmerie often serves the role of an Army Reserve. Should it become necessary, Gendarmerie units can be mobilized and transferred to Army authority on a fairly short notice and become a form of light infantry. (Game note: On a map with a ton of provinces and an insane amount of beaches, a large empire will need a large number of militias in order to stand a chance at defending itself. Militias can be upgraded to garrisons at little cost, or simply disbanded for additional manpower if necessary.)

English: With the Fascist regime deposed in Italy in a royal-military coup, the Armistice of Cassibile soon took effect and provoked widespread fighting between the two main Axis armies in Europe. As the Germans turned on their former ally and attempted to forcibly disarm the Italian army, the Italians were mostly disorganized and demoralized by the events and showed little resistance to the German demands. There were, however, notable exceptions. A few Italian units had put up fierce resistance and ultimately chose to strike a deal with local partisans rather than surrender to the Germans. Up to 30,000 Italians eventually joined the Yugoslav partisans, bringing with them their weapons and experience. Tito then authorized the formation of the first Italian division of the Partisan army in their honor - the Garibaldi division, formed largely from the former soldiers of the Venezia, Bergamo, and Taurinense divisions of the Italian Royal Army.

English: Greece was divided into occupation zones after the defeat of its Royal government by the Axis powers, and only a token collaborationist government was installed to help run the local administration. Nonetheless, up to 22,000 of the so-called 'Security Battalions' militia were eventually raised to help maintain order and combat partisans. The Security Battalions were composed mainly of right-wing republicans and supporters of general Theodoros Pangalos who was the main driving force behind their creation.

The Germans were keenly aware that the Italian defection was imminent and the atmosphere at the military meetings was so tense that the German delegations refused food and beverages offered by the Italians, fearing they would be poisoned.

Meanwhile, the cohesion of the armed forces was quickly faltering and Germany was preparing a major intervention.

English: The new Italian government had moved Mussolini from place to place while he was in captivity in an attempt to foil any attempts at rescue. Despite this, the Germans were able to pinpoint Mussolini and free him in Operation Eiche in the mountains of Abruzzo. After being freed, Mussolini was flown to Bavaria. Gathering what support he still had among the Italian population, his liberation made it possible for a new German-dependent Fascist Italian state to be created.

English: In the days following the armistice, episodes of intolerance and armed resistance against Naples' German occupiers intensified and were more organized, including on 1 September when a student demonstration in Piazza del Plebiscito, and the first meeting of the Liceo Sannazaro in Vomero occurred. Numerous soldiers were killed on the streets of Naples, and about 4,000 Italian soldiers and civilians were deported for forced labor. An announcement on 22 September decreed compulsory labor for all men from 18 to 33, who were to be deported to work camps in northern Italy and Germany. Neapolitans refused, and, as men were rounded up and brought to the stadium in the Vomero, a civilian uprising ensued.

English: On 26 April 1936, Badoglio began the 'March of the Iron Will' from Dessie to Addis Ababa, an advance with a mechanised column against slight Ethiopian resistance. Realizing that Addis Ababa would soon fall to the Italians, Ethiopian administrators met to discuss a possible evacuation of the government to the west. It was decided that the Emperor should go to Geneva to appeal to the League of Nations for assistance before returning to lead resistance. The Italians allowed Emperor Selassie to leave the country by train together with the gold of the Ethiopian Central Bank, and within a week of his departure, Addis Ababa fell to Badoglio's forces. Meanwhile, as the Ethiopian resistance continued in the countryside, Selassie gave a speech in front of the League of Nations. He requested that the League deny recognition of the Italian conquest, maintain the sanctions against Italy, and provide loans to fund the Ethiopian resistance. Both of his motions were defeated, and the League voted to end the sanctions it imposed against Italy in November 1935. Selassie's resolution requesting loans was defeated by a vote of 23 against, 25 abstentions and 1 vote for (from Ethiopia). In the sanctions vote, 44 delegates approved the ending of sanctions, 4 abstained and 1 (Ethiopian) delegate voted for retention. Worldwide, only six nations in 1937 did not recognise the Italian conquest: Mexico, China, New Zealand, the Soviet Union, Spain, and the United States.

It was decided that the Emperor should go to Geneva to appeal to the League of Nations for assistance before returning to lead resistance. The Italians allowed Emperor Selassie to leave the country by train together with the gold of the Ethiopian Central Bank, and within a week of his departure, Addis Ababa fell to Badoglio's forces. Meanwhile, as the Ethiopian resistance continued in the countryside, Selassie gave a speech in front of the League of Nations. He requested that the League deny recognition of the Italian conquest, maintain the sanctions against Italy, and provide loans to fund the Ethiopian resistance. Both of his motions were defeated, and the League voted to end the sanctions it imposed against Italy in November 1935. Selassie's resolution requesting loans was defeated by a vote of 23 against, 25 abstentions and 1 vote for (from Ethiopia). In the sanctions vote, 44 delegates approved the ending of sanctions, 4 abstained and 1 (Ethiopian) delegate voted for retention. Worldwide, only six nations in 1937 did not recognise the Italian conquest: Mexico, China, New Zealand, the Soviet Union, Spain, and the United States.

Most people have been expecting a relatively short and decisive campaign against an African nation described as primitive and incompetent by the Italian press. They were unpleasantly surprised to find their country entangled in a long and bloody struggle with no apparent end in sight. These treasonous attitudes are amplified by the fact that many Italians don't understand this war and don't feel existentially threatened by Ethiopia, so there is a growing lack of enthusiasm for continuing sacrifices which have to be made. The military, the King, and even members of the Fascist Council are advising Mussolini to find a way to end this war quickly as it is proving to be a dangerous drain on the Italian treasury and manpower. If we are not able to achieve our primary goals, they suggest offering a face-saving compromise to Ethiopia as a way out.

English: Italian East Africa was an Italian colony established in 1936, resulting from the merger of the Ethiopian Empire with the colonies of Italian Somaliland and Italian Eritrea. In August 1940, during the Second World War, British Somaliland was conquered and annexed to Italian East Africa, which itself was conquered by British-led forces in the course of 1941. The Ethiopian Empire and British Somaliland were then re-established, while Italian Somaliland and Eritrea both came under British administration. In 1949 Italian Somaliland was reconstituted as the Trust Territory of Somalia, which was administered by Italy from 1949 until its independence in 1960. In 1952 Eritrea was annexed by Ethiopia.

English: With the outbreak of war between Rome and London, England officially recognized the government of the exiled Emperor Haile Selassie and offered it assistance in the re-conquest of his home country. Selassie had the support of a core following of about 5000 fighters who escaped from Ethiopia and were willing to fight under the British flag. But more importantly, Selassie commanded the allegiance of up to 25,000 armed patriot followers known as Arbegnoch, mostly Christians of Amhara and Tigray ethnicity, waging a guerilla war in the mountains of north-western Ethiopia against the Italian occupation.

English:
In December 1935, Chiang Kai-Shek authorized the creation of the Hebei-Chahar Political Council under the leadership of the local strongman Song Zheyuan. Song commanded the NRA's 29th Army based in Hebei and what little was left of Chahar still under NRA control. The goal was to appease Japan by appearing to grant greater autonomy to the northern region, while de-facto keeping the power concentrated in the hands of a trusted general. Thereby Nanjing fulfilled the terms of the He-Umezu Agreement signed earlier in 1935, by which all political organs of the KMT were to be completely withdrawn from Hebei, leaving the 29th Army as the only real organ of power in the region.
 
Japan then proceeded to press Song for further concessions and greater collaboration, but the Chinese General stalled and wavered, always trying to find a compromise but refusing to outright break with Nanjing. While IJA succeed in infiltrating the Council with a number of sympathizers and outright agents, it was never enough to pressure Song into outright collaboration. That is, until Song's most trusted adviser Xiao Zhenying, the Secretary-General of the Hebei-Chahar Council and the Mayor of Tianjin, was found dead outside his residence, shot in the chest by disgruntled officers from the 29th Army's 38th division who fled the scene.
 
§RGame Note:§Z The assassination will trigger if Nanjing suffers serious military defeats OR if the Japanese agents are able to carry it out and blame it on the Chinese nationalist elements. Japan will also be required to invest considerable resources into Hebei to help sway its leadership.

Rumors spread immediately that the hit on Xiao was ordered by Tong Linge, deputy commander of the 29th Army and an unassailable patriot who has long advocated resistance. Xiao, by contrast, was a moderate who favored compromise and conducted negotiations with Japan on Song's behalf. Forged evidence planted by Japanese agents implicated Tong in the assassination on the grounds that Xiao was about to 'sell out' Hebei to the Japanese. A weapon traced to Tong's bodyguard unit was found at the scene.
 
Tokyo's reaction was swift. IJA's Kwantung Army accused anti-Japanese elements within the 29th Army of having murdered a respected statesman and issued an ultimatum to Song, demanding the immediate arrest and court-martial of Tong Linge, removal of all senior officers associated with Tong or with known anti-Japanese records, a public apology and compensation to Xiao's family, and acceptance of Japanese military advisors into the Council's security apparatus to prevent similar incidents in the future.
 
Song Zheyuan did not believe in Tong's guilt, but his options were scarce. With the Chinese public disoriented by the news, the Japanese army mobilized in the north while the pro-Japanese faction in the council seized the moment and urged Song to comply to 'preserve the peace'. Large financial offers were also made by Tokyo to help sway the pragmatists.

English: To save face, Song Zheyuan refused to court-martial Tong Linge. Instead, Tong was dismissed and sent to Nanjing to 'let the civilian authorities carry out the investigation'. The Japanese accepted this as sufficient, given that Song acceeded to most of their key demands. Japanese advisors were stationed in the Council's police and finance bureaus. Officers close to Tong and politicians seen by Tokyo as 'problematic' were dismissed from their posts and their positions were filled by the pro-Japanese loyalists who consolidated control over the Council's daily affairs. While Song remained the nominal leader, effective power shifted towards Wang Kemin who was seen as Tokyo's favorite. Kemin pushed for the Hebei-Chahar council to merge with East Hebei, a neighboring body already under firm Japanese control.\n \nKemin's collaborationism quickly invited resistance, however, as many Chinese, communist and nationalist alike, observed the situation with a mix of fury and dismay, while the 29th Army was unable to come to terms with its apparent capitulation to Japan without a single shot. Tokyo tried to buy off opposition with promises of large investments and assistance, but the Chinese remained deeply skeptical. The 29th Army splintered - several regiments rose up in open rebellion while peasant resistance consolidated in the countryside and attacks on Japanese civilians and businesses intensified. The IJA, predictably, retailated with brutal reprisals. This left Nanjing with no room for compromise. Standing by as the Japanese 'pacified' China's northern capital the same way they have previously 'pacified' Manchuria would mean the end of China as a country. The NRA was ordered to take action and offer assistance to the rebels in Hebei. Thus began the Second Sino-Japanese War.

English: Japanese garrison troops in Feng-Tai, southwest of Beijing, clashed with Chinese forces at the Marco Polo Bridge following an incident involving a Japanese solder who had temporarily gone missing. The battle was at first limited to a local conflict and some hurried negotiations restored order. However, clashes soon resumed with the Langfang Incident, which was followed by a major Tongzhou mutiny that resulted in a massacare of Japanese and Korean civilians. Japan responded with offensive operations - although these were originally limited to the Beijing area. China, however, was no longer in the mood for appeasement and compromise. Chiang Kai Shek ordered a major offensive against the Japanese in Shanghai, and a full scale war began. This seemingly sudden escalation of the frozen conflict was not an accident, but the result of the gradual consolidation of China as well as the successful reconciliation between the two main Chinese parties - KMT and CCP. This all but guaranteed conflict between Japan and China, especially due to the hardline anti-Japanese position of the CCP and its sympathizers. The Chinese simply could not accept the loss of Manchuria and other Japanese gains since 1930, while Japan could not be secure unless it established a protectorate over all of China. The rapprochement between KMT and CCP made the status quo untenable. The choice for Japan now was to either fight or flee. Japan already fled from Russia in 1920s under similar circumstances, could it really afford to show such cowardice again, and miss its possibly last historical chance for greatness?

English:
After securing the main cities and agricultural areas of China, the Japanese general staff believed that they had crippled China's ability to wage war. Yet, the Chinese Army survived, buoyed in large part by the generous support provided by its foreign backers. Beyond the areas already taken lay the vast and largely mountainous hinterland of China. Anything of value that existed within that hinterland was now within the range of Japanese bombers, and could be destroyed from the air. Physically occupying all of China was projected to be extremely costly, pointless, and potentially dangerous, as it could tie up Japan's reserves while simultaneously provoking increased foreign intervention, up to and including outright war against Japan by China's foreign benefactors.
Therefore, the Army General Staff memo of 1940 stated the following: 'China's endurance depends entirely on the continued aid of Britain, the United States, and the Soviet Union.' It was followed by another document which concluded: 'We must remove America's and Britain's hand from China. This cannot be done through further advances inland. With this logic in mind, Tokyo abstained from committing additional reserves into China and instead redireced its main effort towards putting pressure and preparing for war against China's allies.

English: Singapore was the foremost British military base and economic port in South East Asia and had been of great importance to British interwar defence strategy. The Japanese under General Tomoyuki Yamashita had advanced with approximately 30,000 men against at least 85,000 Allied troops dug in the heavily fortified island of Singapore, although many Allied troops were inexperienced and less than reliable. The Japanese managed to surprise the defenders and establish a crossing where they were not expected. A week later, Singapore surrendered. After the battle, about 40,000 Indian soldiers, mostly conscripted, joined the pro-Japanese Indian National Army and later fought with the Japanese in the Burma campaign. Churchill called the defeat at Singapore the worst disaster in British military history.

English: The Japanese occupation was initially greeted with optimistic enthusiasm by Indonesians who came to meet the Japanese army waving flags and shouting support such as 'Japan is our older brother'. As the Japanese advanced, rebellious Indonesians in virtually every part of the archipelago killed groups of Europeans and informed the Japanese reliably on the whereabouts of larger groups. As famed Indonesian writer Pramoedya Ananta Toer noted: 'With the arrival of the Japanese just about everyone was full of hope, except for those who had worked in the service of the Dutch.' In Western Sumatra and in the Aceh region in particular a local Islamic uprising overthrew Dutch rule and welcomed the Japanese. Although a few months later, the same organization fought against Japan as well.

English: After the conquest of Northern China, Japanese Imperial General Headquarters authorized the creation of a collaborationist regime as part of its overall strategy to establish an autonomous buffer zone between China and Japanese-controlled Manchukuo. Initially, this resulted in the creation of local and provincial autonomous administrations, such as the East Hebei Autonomous Government. But plans were drawn up throughout 1937 to unite all of these smaller regimes into one that would serve as a future central government of China. The Provisional Government of the Republic of China was thus officially inaugurated by Wang Kemin, former Kuomintang Minister of Finance and Shanghai banker, with its capital at Beijing. The Provisional Government united smaller pro-Japanese local councils and nominally controlled the provinces of Hebei, Shandong, Shanxi, Henan and Jiangsu. However, the regime's real influence was largely limited to where Japanese military control extended permanently, which meant its jurisdiction was in larger cities and railways.

English: The Free India Legion was a military unit raised during the Second World War initially as part of the German Army in 1942 and later the Waffen-SS from August 1944. Intended to serve as a liberation force for British-ruled India, it was made up of Indian prisoners of war and expatriates in Europe. Owing to its origins in the Indian independence movement, it was known also as the 'Tiger Legion', and the 'Azad Hind Fauj'. As part of the Waffen-SS it was known as the Indian Volunteer Legion of the Waffen-SS.

English: The occupation of Indonesia by Japan for three and a half years during World War II was a crucial factor in the growth of Indonesian nationalism. In Java, and to a lesser extent in Sumatra, the Japanese spread and encouraged Indonesian nationalist sentiment. They created new Indonesian institutions (including local neighbourhood organisations) and elevated political leaders such as Sukarno. Just as significantly, the Japanese destroyed and replaced much of the Dutch-created economic, administrative, and political infrastructure, and promised eventual independence to Indonesia. Meanwhile, Japan also recruited local volunteer units to help defend the islands. The Defenders of the Homeland (PETA) was a volunteer army which consisted of a total of 69 battalions (daidan) by the end of the war, numbering roughly 57,000 men total. In addition, the Japanese also recruited Heiho - an auxillary militia meant mostly for gendarmerie duties. By the end of the war, Heiho numbered some 42,000 men.

English: Upon Hitler's death, the remaining Nazi leaders gathered in Flensburg and made several attempts to negotiate a partial surrender, or, failing that, surrender only to the Western Allies and in doing so provoke a conflict between them and Moscow. On May 4th the Flensburg government signed an instrument of surrender for all remaining forces in northern Europe and Germany. This was accepted by Montgomery on behalf of Eisenhower. This surrender would become effective at 8:00 am on May 5th, and it was joined by the remaining German forces trapped in South-west Germany as well, thus including all German forces on the Western Front. Meanwhile, the troops facing the Soviet Army were ordered to continue resistance, and where possible, westward evacuation. The Allies quickly caught on to the German plan, and Eisenhower declared that hostilities would resume unless Germany declared immediate unconditional surrender on all fronts. Should the Germans continue to stall for time, the Allies would shoot at any German trying to surrender, and any future surrenders would have to be made to the Soviets instead. Faced with these options, Germany had no choice but to acceed to Allied demands. The German military leadership ended up signing two more surrender documents before hostilities definitively ceased. One was signed on May 7th, but was not consulted with the Soviet side and was thus scrapped on the same day. The second, ammended surrender document was signed on May 8th shortly before midnight Berlin time. On May 9, Donitz issued orders to the German Armed Forces regarding the military surrender and the World War II in Europe officially ended. The Allies dissolved the Flensburg government a month later.

English: The Potsdam Conference was a meeting of the Big Three Allied leaders to decide the future of post-World War II Europe. The key participants were Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill (later replaced by Clement Attlee), and Harry S. Truman. The conference addressed the administration of defeated Germany, establishing the postwar order, resolving issues related to peace treaties, and planning the continued war against Japan. Notably, France was not represented at the conference, which became a long standing point of tension in relations with Paris.

English: The Allied Control Council was the governing body of the Allied occupation zones in Germany and Austria following the end of World War II in Europe. Its members (Four-Power Authorities)  were the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, the United States, and France. The Allied Control Council asserted itself as the sole legal sovereign authority for Germany and Austria, replacing the civil government under the Nazi Party. In 1948, the Soviets withdrew from the ACC due to its conflict with the western Allies, who then established the Allied High Commission.

English: At the Yalta Conference held earlier, Stalin pledged that the Soviet Union would enter the Pacific War within three months after the defeat of Germany. In return, the Soviets wanted the return of South Sakhalin, which had been taken from Russia by Japan in the Russo-Japanese War in 1905, and the cession of Kuril Islands by Japan, both of which were approved by the other Allies. In addition, the Allies recognized independence of the Mongolian People's Republic from China, the Soviet interests in Manchuria, and discussed the possible future of Korea, with Roosevelt bringing up the idea of putting Korea into a trusteeship divided among the Soviets, the Americans, and the Chinese for a period of 20 to 30 years.

English: Bizonia, also referred to as the Bizone, was established on January 1, 1947, during the Allied occupation of Germany following World War II. This entity was formed by the economic merger of the American and British occupation zones in Germany. The goal behind the Bizone's creation was to stimulate economic recovery and establish a stable political order in the western parts of Germany, which included the states of Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg, Lower Saxony, Bremen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Hesse, Bavaria, and the northern portion of Baden-Wurttemberg. The Bizone's creation represented a crucial step in the post-war reconstruction of Germany and marked the initial stage in the country's division into two separate states, East and West Germany. It laid the foundation for the eventual creation of the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany).

English: Bizonia, also referred to as the Bizone, was established on January 1, 1947, during the Allied occupation of Germany following World War II. This entity was formed by the economic merger of the American and British occupation zones in Germany. On August 1, 1948, the French occupation zone joined the Bizone, transforming it into the Trizone, or Trizonia. This unification further consolidated the Western Allied zones and paved the way for West Germany's establishment. The Trizone officially became the Federal Republic of Germany on May 23, 1949. France, however, made sure to exclude the Saar region from the Trizone.

English: The Greek insurgency was largely destroyed by the bitter split between Stalin and Tito. In June 1948, the Soviet Union and its satellites broke off relations with Yugoslavia, and all members of the Cominform were forced to pick a side. Although Yugoslavia seemed like a more practical choice, given the crucial lifeline of military aid it provided to the DSE, the USSR was still the undisputed ideological and military center of the Communist world. Breaking with the USSR would have meant a tremendous loss in internal legitimacy, isolation in case of a wider war, along with a myriad of other problems. It would have also meant unconditional subordination to Tito, an ambitious neighbor with obvious designs on Greek territory. After some internal conflict, the great majority, led by party secretary Nikolaos Zachariadis, chose to follow the Soviet Union. In January 1949, Vafiadis was removed from his political and military positions, to be replaced by Zachariadis, who initiated a witch hunt for 'Titoites' in the KKE that demoralised and disorganised the ranks of the DSE and sapped support for the insurgency in urban areas. After a year of increasing acrimony, Tito closed the Yugoslav border to the DSE and disbanded its camps inside Yugoslavia. At the same time, the National Army received a new lifeline of military aid and found a talented commander in General Alexander Papagos, commander of the Greek Army during the Greco-Italian War. In August 1949, Papagos launched a major offensive against the demoralized DSE forces in northern Greece. By September 1949, the main body of DSE divisions defending Grammos and Vitsi, the two key positions in northern Greece, had retreated to Albania. The were followed by an exhodus or Slavic refugees who mostly aided the insurgency and were afraid of the reprisals.

English: After a year of see-saw fighting, the war has reached an impasse. Fierce fighting continued between the UN and the PVA/KPA but little territory was exchanged. North Korea was being devastated by large scale bombing, but to little immediate effect since the real power behind the Communist effort remained untouched. Meanwhile the communist insurgency, reinvigorated by North Korean support and scattered bands of KPA stragglers, resurged in the south. Protracted armistice negotiations began in July 1951 and spanned over two years, with the most problematic aspect being the prisoner of war repatriation. Stalin died on 5 March 1953. The new Soviet leaders, engaged in their internal power struggle, had no desire to continue supporting China's efforts and called for an end to the hostilities. The armistice agreement was finally signed on 27 July 1953. The belligerents established the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) which mostly follows the 38th parallel, but no peace treaty was established.

English: At the Potsdam and Moscow Conferences, the Allies agreed to divide Indochina along the 16th parallel to allow the Allies to enter and disarm the Japanese army. The Chinese took responsibility for the North, while the British and French were to take control of the south. However, there was a third player - the Democratic Republic of Vietnam (DRV), led by Ho Chi Minh, which de-facto controlled most of the country. As the Allies started to enter the south, they immediately began clashing with the DRV forces (Vietminh) positioned in and around Saigon. In the North, however, the situation was different. Despite the ideological differences and fear of Chinese domination, Ho Chi Minh felt that he could not afford to fight both the Chinese and the Europeans at the same time, and decided to play them off against each other. With China weakened by its own domestic turbulance for the forseeable future, Ho Chi Minh resolved to appease the Chinese, seeing them as a lesser immediate threat. Vietminh organized parades in honor of the Chinese soldiers and even agreed to help pay for the Chinese occupation.

English: After several months of fighting, Vietminh decided to change strategy. In a surprise diplomatic reversal rivaling Molotov-Ribbentrop, Ho Chi Minh signed an agreement with Jean Sainteny, the French commissioner for Indochina, in which DRV agreed to become an autonomous part of the new 'French Union', largely sovereign but with some lingering French control and military presense. Overnight, Vietminh went from being an enemy of France to its ally. The agreement ultimately fell through, and fighting between the two sides resumed after a lull of about 9 months, neither side being fully satisfied with the terms. The signing, however, made sense for both parties. For Vietminh, the agreement meant consolidating power at the expense of the Chinese and their pro-KMT domestic allies, gaining legitimacy, and buying cruicial time for the nanscent DRV forces to prepare for the inevitable conflict. For France, the agreement allowed peaceful reentry into Tonkin, removal of the Chinese, division in the Vietnamese nationalist movement, and also time - for the greatly weakened French Army to reconstitute itself in the aftermath of WW2 and take on the full burden of the war as the British gradually withdrew from Indochina. Chiang, for his part, had little interest in committing troops to the occupation of Indochina when they were badly needed at home, and he was easily convinced to withdraw in exchange for the French surrendering all of their concessions and ports in China. This left the pro-KMT Vietnamese (VNQDD) without support, and they were suppressed by Vietminh and French troops. The Vietminh then massacred thousands of VNQDD members and other right-wing nationalists in a large-scale purge.

English: After the surrender of Japan, Prince Phetsarath and several other Lao nationalists formed 'Free Laos' (Lao Issara) in the power vacuum, which took control of the government and declared independence in defiance of the French. The government was non-Communist, but allied to Vietminh, however it was also very weak and lacked a solid rural base. It quickly ran out of money, was unable to raise a proper army, and could do little but await the inevitable French return. At the end of April 1946, the French took Vientiane, and by May, they had entered Luang Prabang, and the Lao Issara leadership fled into exile in Thailand. Many of the surviving fighters of the 'Free Laos' later joined Pathet Lao, Vietminh, and other Communist organizations.

English: Ever since the Communists gained power in China, the military situation in Indochina has been looking worse day after day. The enemy is rapidly growing in strength while slowly draining our manpower and financial resources. The opinion in France has turned completely against the war, with the populace and the elites alike increasingly feeling that the far away colony is not even remotely worth the sacrifices that France would have to pay to keep it under control. Meanwhile, another colonial crisis is rapidly brewing in Algeria, which is far more vital to French security, and we need to get ready to deal with this emerging threat. On the other side, emboldened by their experience in Korea, the Americans are eager to get involved in Indochina - but not to buttress the French rule, which they see as unjust, unpopular, and more importantly - inefficient and counterproductive. They want to strike an alliance with the Vietnamese nationalist forces led by Ngo Dinh Diem, who are staunchly anti-Communist, but also vehemently opposed to the French rule. Should we agree, Vietnam will be temporarily divided in half along the 17th parallel. Vietminh will consolidate its rule over the north, while Americans will protect the south. Laos and Cambodia will also be de-facto in the American sphere, except for a few border areas. This may be our best bet for a face-saving way to exit this conflict.

Seeing that time is against them, the French desperately tried to provoke a decisive battle at Dien Bein Phu, and ended up suffering a humiliating defeat. The experience of Korea shows that the struggle against the Americans is bound to be long and bloody - possibly more so than the war against the French. Our exhausted soldiers are not yet ready for this struggle, and more importantly, our allies are not ready for it either. We will consolidate our rule over the north, while Americans will dominate the rest. Elections are to be held in both halves, but Ho Chi Minh's immense popularity combined with the North's slight population advantage means we are likely to win a free election - should it ever be held. English: The French have given up on the war in Indochina. Short on manpower and financial resources, and with another colonial crisis rapidly brewing in Algeria, they are getting out. The north is lost, and only a fool would want to fight a battle so close to the Chinese border. However, we cannot allow the Communits have have a full victory, either. If Vietnam falls, the entire region may go to the Reds. We may not be able to recover the north, but we've shown that we can bleed the Communists to a standstill in Korea, and if need be, we can do it again in Vietnam. With the French on their way out, we can now strike an alliance with the Vietnamese nationalist forces led by Ngo Dinh Diem, who are staunchly anti-Communist, but also vehemently opposed to the French rule. Should we agree, Vietnam will be temporarily divided in half along the 17th parallel. Vietminh will consolidate its rule over the north, while we will protect the rest, including Laos and Cambodia, except for a few border areas. It's an option we can live with.

English: Syria and France negotiated a treaty of independence in September 1936. France agreed to Syrian independence in principle although maintained French military and economic dominance. However, the treaty never came into force because the French Legislature refused to ratify it. With the fall of France during World War II, Syria remained under the control of Vichy France until the British and Free French occupied the country in the Syria-Lebanon campaign in July 1941. Syria proclaimed its independence again in 1941, but it was not until 1 January 1944 that it was recognised as an independent republic. The slow pace of French withdrawal triggered protests that escalated into armed clashes and mass civilian casualties as the French troops occupied the Syrian parliament and cut off the electricity to Damascus in an effort to stop the movement toward independence. However, the British troops then invaded Syria and forced the weaker French army to cease operations and return to their barracks. Under strong pressure from the British and Syrian nationalist groups, the French were forced to evacuate the last of their troops in April 1946, leaving the country in the hands of a republican government that had been formed during the mandate.

English: With the fall of France during World War II, Lebanon remained under the control of Vichy France until the British and Free French occupied the country in the Syria-Lebanon campaign in July 1941. After the fighting ended in Lebanon, General Charles de Gaulle visited the area. Under various political pressures from both inside and outside Lebanon, de Gaulle decided to recognize the independence of Lebanon. On 26 November 1941, General Georges Catroux announced that Lebanon would become independent under the authority of the Free French government. Elections were held in 1943 and on 8 November 1943, the new Lebanese government unilaterally abolished the mandate. The French reacted by throwing the new government into prison. In the face of international pressure, the French released the government officials on 22 November 1943, and accepted the independence of Lebanon. The last French troops withdrew in 1946.

English: Although a League of Nations mandate was awarded to the United Kingdom in 1920, the 1920 Iraqi revolt resulted in the scrapping of the original mandate plan in favour of a formally sovereign Iraqi kingdom, but one that was under effective British administration. The plan was formally established by the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty. The role of the United Kingdom in the formal administration of the Kingdom of Iraq was ended in 1932, following the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty (1930). Now officially a fully independent kingdom, officially named the Hashemite Kingdom of Iraq, it underwent a period of turbulence under its Hashemite rulers throughout its entire existence. During the Second World War, the Iraqi government of the Prince-Regent, Prince Abd al-Ilah, was overthrown in 1941 by the Golden Square officers, headed by Rashid Ali. The short-lived pro-Axis government of Iraq was defeated in May 1941 by the Allied forces in the Anglo-Iraqi War. In 1945, during the final stages of World War II, Iraq joined the United Nations and became a founding member of the Arab League.

The role of the United Kingdom in the formal administration of the Kingdom of Iraq was ended in 1932, following the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty (1930). Now officially a fully independent kingdom, officially named the Hashemite Kingdom of Iraq, it underwent a period of turbulence under its Hashemite rulers throughout its entire existence. During the Second World War, the Iraqi government of the Prince-Regent, Prince Abd al-Ilah, was overthrown in 1941 by the Golden Square officers, headed by Rashid Ali. The short-lived pro-Axis government of Iraq was defeated in May 1941 by the Allied forces in the Anglo-Iraqi War. In 1945, during the final stages of World War II, Iraq joined the United Nations and became a founding member of the Arab League.

English: The UN General Assembly passed a resolution proposing partition of Mandatory Palestine between a Jewish and Arab Palestinian states, with Jerusalem as a special extraterritorial zone. The Arab state was to end up with only 42 percent of the territory, despite having a population of over two thirds the size of the Jewish population, and with the overwhelming majority of the Jewish population being recent immigrants post-1918. The plan was supported by the key major players - USSR, USA, as well as France, though Britain abstained from the vote. The Muslim states, and the Palestinians themselves, found this lopsided proposal to be completely unacceptable, and vowed to fight against it. A few non-Muslim states publicly supported the Palestinian position, key among them was India, whose leader Nehru spoke at length about the bribes and threats he was subjected to in attempt to make him change his stance. The Arab nations surrounding Palestine then decided to intervene forcefully in the matter as soon as the British troops withdrew. Behind their rhetoric, however, was a much more practical interest. Each of the Arab rulers was hoping to secure for himself new land in Palestine, and above all, check the ambitions of other Arab leaders and prevent them from gaining a dominant position. The key competition was between the Kings of Egypt (backed by Syria) and Jordan (backed by Iraq), with both leaders more afraid of each other than of Israel. With their interests revolving mostly around sabotaging each other's efforts, their committment to the actual Palestinian cause was minimal and their cooperation practically non-existent.
