English: USSR voted alongside the United States for Resolution 181 which advised for the withdrawal of British troops from Palestine and its partition between a Jewish majority and Arab majority states. The Arab countries in the region, however, rejected the resolution, and guided by a mix of personal ambitions and a desire to expand their territories, they have sent their troops in to Palestine the moment British forces began to withdraw. The irony is, however, that some of those Arab states remain very closesly tied to Britain, so much so that the top leadership of the Jordanian Army, for example, is British. If the Jewish state were to fall, in effect this would mean the restoration of British power in the region but by new means. The Arab regimes in the region are ruled by backward monarchs who are deeply hostile to the Soviet Union. Israel, by contrast, could eventually become an ally, or at least a non-aligned power, if we play our cards right. We should be careful to keep our involvement low profile, however, as we do not want to upset our own Muslim populations or permanently ruin relations with our Muslim neighbors.

English: Although the official US position with respect to the conflict was one of neutrality, there was a lot of sympathy in the US for the Israeli cause from the very beginning, helped in part by its very influential Jewish community. It only makes sense that we should do the same, for if we do not, we will leave a ticking time bomb under the very foundation of our State.

English: After a protracted struggle, neither side was able to secure a decisive victory in Palestine. The Arabs were not able to dislodge the Jews from their main strongholds in Haifa and Tel Aviv, but the Jews were also not able to kick out the Arab armies from Palestine either. Under these conditions, the Arab High Committee proposed to freeze the conflict along the lines resembling those originally proposed by the UN commission. The original plan had the city of Jaffa right next to Tel Aviv assigned as an Arab exclave, while southern Negev was assigned to Israel for 'future settlement'. Given the military reality on the ground, the Arab Committee proposes for Jaffa to go to Israel while Egypt will keep southern Negev.

English: Having just emerged from a disasterous war in Indochina, France was immediately faced with not one or two but three simultenous crises brewing in North Africa. There is very little chance that we can handle all three at the same time. Out policymakers are strongly advising that we resolve the matters in Morocco and Tunisia peacefully be giving into as much of insurgent demands as needed in order to preserve the peace, and concentrate all our military efforts on Algeria - the biggest, richest, and most important of our posessions in North Africa both strategically and politically. Unlike Morocco and Tunisia, from which we can withdraw with relatively little domestic reprecussions, Algeria is different. Algeria has a very large ethnic French minority, concentrated around the coastal cities, and it is legally not a colony, but an integral part of France. Giving up Algeria without a fight is practically unthinkable.

English: Having just emerged from a devastating Civil War and isolation following defeat of the Axis powers, Franco was in no mood to get stuck in a protracted colonial crisis in Morocco, certainly not without French help. When France, hit by the humiliation of Indochina and three simultaneous crises in North Africa, decided to abandon Morocco, Franco realized that he needed to urgently make a deal as well. Luckily, some moderate Moroccan forces around King Muhammed and the Istiqlal Party were amenable to a compromise. While fighting continued around Ifni and insurency raged in the Rif, the two sides worked out a deal where Spain would cede most of the densely populated Moroccan lands to the King, but would retain control of certain strategic coastal towns of mixed population - including Ceuta and Melilla, the town of Sidi Ifni (although without its countryside), and most of Spanish Morocco.

English: As the Germans withdrew their forces westward, they left behind a number of insurgent militias who benefitted directly or indirectly from the occupation. Aside from the Partisans, most of them did not look kindly at the return of the Soviet government. One of such militias was UPA, formed from the merger of two Ukrainian nationalist organizations OUN-B and OUN-M. UPA attempted to resist the restoration of Soviet rule in western Ukraine and waged an active insurgency for about a year until the dominant presense of the Soviet security apparatus forced them to significantly scale back their activities. UPA then switched to a low level insurgency which continued into the 1950s until the organization was completely suppressed.

The default yearly GNP growth rate is §H5\%§Z.
Developing countries get a boost of §G+0.5\%§Z per development level, up to §G+4.5\%§Z at maximum.
Countries rapidly recovering from the 1929 Depression (primarily Germany and USA) get §B+4\%§Z for up to 6 years.
War economy subtracts §C-1\%§Z GNP growth per level, up to §C-9\%§Z at maximum.
Non-sanctioned market economies will take foreign credit to fund higher levels of economic mobilization, decreasing the impact of war economy by §N+0.5\%§Z per level, up to §N+2.5\%§Z at maximum, but will also accumulate debt over time. Debt accumulation will cause a reduction of future GNP growth rates due to increased interest burden. Debt will be repaid gradually when the war economy slider is below 5.
Economic sanctions imposed by the US and UK will cause a one-time GNP reduction of §F-8\%§Z, and will continue to depress future growth by §F-1\%§Z per year.

English:
Our central bank has accumulated sizable reserves of foreign currency and precious metals. We can now choose how to spend these reserves in such a way as to produce the most benefit to our nation.
 
-Investment in §HPropaganda§Z will convince the population that our cause is just, decreasing our unrest by §H-3\%§Z.
-Investment in §GGrowth§Z will subsidize new industries and startups, boosting our total economic output by §G+2\%§Z.
-Investment in §BInfrastructure§Z will improve our rail network (§B+0.5\%§Z) and boost economic output (§B+0.5\%§Z)
-Investment in §CEducation§Z will improve research speed (§C+0.5\%§Z) and boost economic output (§C+0.5\%§Z)
-Investment in §NTraining§Z will increase the skills of our officers and boost the organization of our land, sea, and air forces by §N+0.5\%§Z
-Investment in §RRecruitment§Z will attract new contractors and volunteers to the military, increasing our manpower pool. Recruitment becomes progressively §Rless effective§Z at higher levels of §Rmobilization§Z, and will yield less additional manpower.
-Investment in §FDiplomacy§Z will yield blueprints for new technologies, reduce our belligerence level by §F-6\%§Z, and improve our relations with other countries by §F+30§Z. Reducing belligerence may make it politically difficult for our potential adversaries to maintain a high levels of peacetime defense spending.
-Investment in §YMedicine§Z will increase the suvivability of our troops in harsh environments (§Y+2\%§Z) and increase the number of wounded soldiers who can return to active service (§Y+1\%§Z).

Their power substantially increased in September with the rise of Antonescu. However, once in power, Sima and Antonescu quarreled bitterly. Antonescu intended to follow the footsteps of Francisco Franco in Spain, and have the Legion fully subordinated to the state. He demanded that Sima cede overall leadership of the Legion to him, but Sima had opposite plans. Sima demanded that the government follow the 'legionary spirit', and all major offices be held by legionaries. Other groups were to be dissolved. After securing personal support from Hitler, Antonescu began gradually revoking the Iron Guard privileges. The latter responded with increasingly chaotic violence. Finally, a murder incident in Bucharest triggered an armed confrontation between the Legionnaires and the Army, backed by Antonescu.

English: At the beginning of the revolt in July, General Jose Sanjurjo, in exile in Portugal, was recognized as a leader and would-be 'Caudillo' of the rebel faction. However, he died on 20 July in a plane crash, while attempting to fly back to Spain. This left the revolt without a clear leader. A collective leadership body was then established, known as National Defense Junta, under the nominal leadership of Miguel Cabanellas, the most senior participating general. General Emilio Mola, the main 'Director' of the uprising and commander of the Nationalist forces in the north, was the second most prominent figure in the Junta. Francisco Franco was added to the council later in early August. The Junta immediately began bickering and was unable to set an overall strategy. Being career officers, all of the Junta members implicitly recognized that the army cannot be led by a collective leadership - there has to be a single leader of the armed forces, and a single future Caudillo of Spain. Thus, in September 1936, the Junta met to decide on a leader once and for all. Cabanellas was not favored for this role as he was too old, too moderate and a Freemason on top of that. Mola was a likelier candidate, but he was seen as too ruthless and radical, and his chief role as the planner of the coup earned him some derision as the coup effectively failed and degenerated into a bloody civil war. Ultimately, Francisco Franco was chosen near-unanimously as a 'compromise candidate' who showed great promise as the leader of the Army of Africa, had little prior involvement in politics, good military credentials, and support from the Catholic Church.

English: After the Popular Front victory in the February elections, the Republic went through a series of moderate-left minority governments, each one making successive attempts to reach a national consensus, restore order, and avoid a coup. Some lasted only 3 days in office, others just 1 day, and none were successful. The cabinet of Jose Giral lasted 47 days, but as the reality of the military uprising became an unavoidable fact and with the Republican forces suffering one setback after another, Jose Giral's government had no choice but to resign in order to make way for a broad-based coalition of left-wing parties supporting the Republic, including the Communists, Socialists, and Anarchists. The Popular Front coalition, which included a broad spectrum of leftist parties, called for a government that better represented the revolutionary zeal of the masses and could implement more decisive measures needed to transform Spanish society and win the war. In these circumstances, Francisco Largo Caballero, a charismatic socialist leader and former head of the General Union of Workers (UGT-PSOE), emerged as the key figure capable of uniting the leftist factions. Initially hailed as the 'Spanish Lenin', Caballero quickly formed a government that included all the chief left-wing parties. Thus, the civil war turned into the 'battle of two Franciscos'. One of the first contraversial decisions of the Caballero government was to transfer all of Spain's gold reserves outside the country - 75% to USSR and the remaining 25% to France. Caballero's candidacy was opposed by Prieto Tuero, another popular leader of the PSOE and a representative of its moderate wing, as well as Juan Negrin, another moderate, who nonetheless enjoyed very close ties to the USSR and the support of the local Communist Party.

English: While both sides of the conflict in Spain experienced some level of economic hardship, nothing compared to the utter financial chaos that gripped the Republican-held areas starting in 1937. On the surface, nothing seemed to indicate the coming economic catastrophe. Republicans started the war in control of many major developed industrial centers, sizable gold reserves of the Spanish central bank, the privelege of being recognized as a legitimate government of Spain, foreign backing of the Soviet Union and sympathizers in many other countries. The reasons behind the crisis are still not completely understood, and much blame is laid at the feet of the Madrid government, the revolutionary militias, and Moscow. While the Francoist side developed a pragmatic approach to the economy which proved relatively successful, the Republican side faced unyielding pressure from within to transform the Spanish economy in the midst of a war, and it ended up with massive distortions and inability to collect taxes. The process of collectivizations and nationalizations, aimed at developing a socialist economy for the post-war period, has been pointed to as the cause for this situation as most of the taxable economic agents were eradicated. Banks stopped paying interest and were expropriated, rents were not collected anymore, collectivized factories distributed their earnings among their workers and were therefore permanently decapitalized, and public limited companies stopped paying dividends. Republican collectivizations also had a lasting effect on the tourism sector, as the socialization of hotels, cafes, restaurants and spectacle venues led to a complete paralysis of the activity. Meanwhile, despite the Republic's status as an internationally recognized government, most foreign businesses began to avoid the Republican areas, afraid of having their assets arbitrarily nationalized or simply ransacked and stolen. Where possible, they redirected their trade to the Nationalist zone instead. In the end, the only way Madrid could continue to fund the war effort was through massive monetary emission, which resulted in equally massive hyperinflation, reaching 200 to 300 percent. This, in turn, led to the improverishment of the Spanish populace, disillusionment and demoralization, blame trading, infighting, and ultimately, to defeat. By 1938, the Republican Treasury had lost all its collection power and the country was left in a year of absolute fiscal anarchy, with rampant inflation and deficit. Civil servants gradually started going away and the Treasury directive board stopped holding its meetings.

English: Over time, the Spanish economy began to gradually adjust to the new conditions. The unruly revolutionary militias were cracked down upon or integrated into the Armed Forces, a new tax code was implemented, a black market made up for the shortages of consumer goods, some of the revolutionary excesses were undone, and the currency situation somewhat stabilized. The Spanish economy thus started its long journey towards recovery. Madrid called it the 'New Economic Policy', modeled after Lenin's successful recovery program in the USSR after its civil war.

English: Since the defeat of the military uprising in Barcelona, the city and the rest of Catalonia and Aragon fell into de-facto control of various local militias, most of them associated with the Anarchist organizations CNT and FAI. Initially, the militia leaders established the Central Committee of Antifascist Militias of Catalonia as the main governing body which held dual power with the Generalitat of Catalonia. In September, an agreement was reached by which the Central Committee became an official a part of Generalitat under a new name - Internal Security Junta of Catalonia. While theoretically subordinate to the Generalitat, the head of the Generalitat Lluis Companys had little effective control over the organization and could not even speak with Madrid without the Junta dictating what he can and cannot say. Furthermore, the Internal Security Junta was itself disunited and had only loose control over its constituent parts. One such part which was proving particularly troublesome was the so-called worker's 'Control Patrols', which became the new de-facto police force in Barcelona. In this capacity they routinely engaged in violence and performed arbitrary expropriations, arrests, and executions in the name of 'revolutionary justice'. Any attempt to reign in the 'Control Patrols' was proving futile, despite the fact that the Control Patrols themselves numbered no more than 700 people. Behind them, however, there was a wider struggle developing between different wings of the republican movement. On one side was the alliance of the moderate 'social democrats' and Stalinists, on the other - anarchists and Trostskyists. One on side were believiers in a strong, centralized Spanish state, on the other - supporters of Catalonian autonomy and decentralization. English: While the Trotskyist POUM and many local Anarchist militia groups advocated armed resistance, the majority of the Anarchist CNT was absolutely frightened by the possibility of war against both Burgos and Madrid at the same time. Instead, the CNT leaders repeatedly appealed to the militias to end the violence and allow the police to do its work. Lluis Companys and his ERC, likewise, had little appetite for a second uprising against Madrid - after the first one thoroughly failed in 1934. Meanwhile, a new force of about 5,000 policemen departed from Madrid and Valencia towards Barcelona. Two Republican destroyers and the battleship Jaime I, coming from Valencia, reached the port of Barcelona on the same day. That night, Lluis Companys had a conversation with Caballero and accepted Madrid's 'offer of assistance' in restoring order. An inter-republican civil war was narrowly avoided. However, while the clashes soon stopped, the consequences of the events in Catalonia were far-reaching. One of the casualties was Trotskyist POUM, which was promptly outlawed at the insistence of USSR, and its leaders arrested. Another casualty was Francisco Caballero himself, who was accused of mishandling the Barcelona crisis. The Stalinists in particular also saw a good opportunity to scapegoat Caballero for all the frontline setbacks and economic failures. As a result, they pulled their support from the Caballero government, and the Prime Minister was forced to resign. His replacement, Juan Negrin, was from the same party as Caballero, but he was seen as a more moderate figure, and simultaneously even more beholden to the Soviets - who at this time preferred to place their bets on the moderates rather than radical revolutionaries.

Lluis Companys and his ERC, likewise, had little appetite for a second uprising against Madrid - after the first one thoroughly failed in 1934. Meanwhile, a new force of about 5,000 policemen departed from Madrid and Valencia towards Barcelona. Two Republican destroyers and the battleship Jaime I, coming from Valencia, reached the port of Barcelona on the same day. That night, Lluis Companys had a conversation with Caballero and accepted Madrid's 'offer of assistance' in restoring order. An inter-republican civil war was narrowly avoided. However, while the clashes soon stopped, the consequences of the events in Catalonia were far-reaching. One of the casualties was Trotskyist POUM, which was promptly outlawed at the insistence of USSR, and its leaders arrested. Another casualty was Francisco Caballero himself, who was accused of mishandling the Barcelona crisis. The Stalinists in particular also saw a good opportunity to scapegoat Caballero for all the frontline setbacks and economic failures. As a result, they pulled their support from the Caballero government, and the Prime Minister was forced to resign. His replacement, Juan Negrin, was from the same party as Caballero, but he was seen as a more moderate figure, and simultaneously even more beholden to the Soviets - who at this time preferred to place their bets on the moderates rather than radical revolutionaries.

English: Since the defeat of the military uprising in the Basque region, much of the Basque country fell under de-facto control of the PNV - a Basque Nationalist party. PNV's alliance with the Republican government in Madrid was always somewhat of an odd coaltion - a conservative, Catholic, separatist party in alliance with a left-wing radical centralist government dominated by radical socialists and stalinists - it was always an alliance of pure convinience. On the surface, the PNV seemed to have much more in common with the Carlists. Indeed, not too long ago, the Carlists and Basque nationalists were allied to each other in the Cortes, and when the military uprising broke out in 1936, both of them initially hesitated and did not find either side very appealing. Ultimately, however, they ended up on the opposite sides of the frontline. The Carlists joined the military uprising, lulled in part by promises of broad regional autonomy, while the Basque nationalists decided to resist it. The PNV then went about forming a regional government in coalition with the Republican parties - including the socialists and communits. The government was dominated by the PNV and led by the President (Lehendakari) Jose Antonio Aguirre, who also served as minister of defence. Although the government did not formally declare its independence from Spain, in everything but formality it was a sovereign state - the first such Basque statehood in Spain's history. But as the civil war progressed, inherent contradictions in PNV's alliance with Madrid began to mount. While Madrid was willing to put up with some Basque autonomy especially for the duration of the war, it was completely and firmly against PNV's separatist agenda. Meanwhile the left-wing parties in the Cortes openly decried PNV as reactionary and even fascist due to its defense of Catholicism, private property, and traditional values. Eventually, the Basque government had to face the same ultimatum which was presented to Catalonia earlier. Madrid demanded submission and de-facto control in Bilbao. Absent that, there was a high risk of clashes between the pro-Republican parties and the PNV.

The government was dominated by the PNV and led by the President (Lehendakari) Jose Antonio Aguirre, who also served as minister of defence. Although the government did not formally declare its independence from Spain, in everything but formality it was a sovereign state - the first such Basque statehood in Spain's history. But as the civil war progressed, inherent contradictions in PNV's alliance with Madrid began to mount. While Madrid was willing to put up with some Basque autonomy especially for the duration of the war, it was completely and firmly against PNV's separatist agenda. Meanwhile the left-wing parties in the Cortes openly decried PNV as reactionary and even fascist due to its defense of Catholicism, private property, and traditional values. Eventually, the Basque government had to face the same ultimatum which was presented to Catalonia earlier. Madrid demanded submission and de-facto control in Bilbao. Absent that, there was a high risk of clashes between the pro-Republican parties and the PNV.

English: After many months of tiresome negotiations, Franco produced a 'Unification Decree' - effectively an ultimatum, ordering both Falange and the Carlist Communion to dissolve and to merge into a single political party, headed by Franco himself. Faced with the ultimatum, many leaders of both the Carlists and the Falange were dismayed. Some dared to oppose the decree - and were swiftly jailed or exiled. There were some instances of riots and clashes, but on the whole, neither the Carlists nor the Falange, particularly their rank-and-file, had any appetite for an inter-Nationalist civil war. Many of the main Carlist and Falangist leaders were coopted or outright bought off, and included within the council of the new ruling party, named FET de la JONS. Most of the militias likewise fell in line, albeit will very little enthusiasm. The new mandated militia uniform was to combine the blue shirt of the Falange and the red cap of the Carlists. Most of the Alfonists and regular conservatives likewise joined Franco's new sole legal political movement.

Many Basques supported the Carlists due to their advocacy for the restoration of traditional privileges, or fueros, which had been curtailed by liberal governments. This contrasted with urban centers like Bilbao, where leftist and nationalist sentiments were more common.

English: After the fall of Bilbao, almost all of Basque territory had fallen into Franco's hands. Juan de Ajuriaguerra, the president of the Biscay Regional Council of the PNV, negotiated a surrender agreement with the Italian army command. The PNV offered to surrender the Basque army in exchange of its prisoners being treated as prisoners-of-war under Italian command and PNV members being allowed to go to exile on British ships. The Basque nationalist units of the Republican army in the Basque territory, fighting under the direction of Basque President Jose Antonio Aguirre, met at Santona and surrendered to the Italian forces. When news of the agreement arrived to his headquarters, Franco cancelled the agreement and ordered the immediate jailing of the 22,000 captured soldiers in Santona's El Dueso Prison. Three months later, around half of them had been freed, and the other half remained in prison, and 510 were sentenced to death, a smaller proportion than registered in reprisals elsewhere. Ajuriaguerra, the highest ranked member of the PNV, was released from prison in 1943. While the surrender affected the Basque fighters loyal to the PNV, there were many Basques who rejected the agreement and chose to continue the fight. The included primarily the left-leaning Basques affiliated with the PCE, PSOE, or other left wing parties.

English: After the surrender of main Basque forces and the fall of Santander, Eastern Asturias was the last piece of Republican-held territory in the north. As the Republican offensive on Zaragoza in failed to result in a meaningful breakthrough, the Nationalists decided to finish off the remaining Republican forces in the Asturias. The Nationalist force of 90,000 men, with support from the Condor Legion and the Corps of Volunteer Troops, attacked the Republican force of 45,000 men composed of Spanish Republican Army soldiers and allied CNT militias from two directions. The Republicans resisted the much larger Nationalist force until mid-September when their lines were broken and began to lose territory to further offensives. The Nationalist capture of Gijon in late October saw the end of Republican occupation in northern Spain and the end of the War in the North. Madrid ordered the evacuation of Asturias on October 17, but due to remoteness and Nationalist naval superiority only about 15,000–20,000 people were evacuated by sea from Asturias to France or other Republican areas before the final fall of the north.

English: Following the success of the latest Nationalist offensive, the Republic was in dire straits. Almost three years since the start of the military coup, and victory seemed further than ever. All attempts to rectify the situation, even the huge and bloody Ebro Offensive, had failed to yield any meaningful gains. Even worse news, however, came not from the battlefiled, but from the foreign capitals. The failure of France and England to defend Czhechoslovakia had dashed the main loyalist hope that a European war would force the Allied armies to intervene and rescue the Republic. Following this, the Soviets started to pull back aid as well. This had a serious effect of the morale of the Republican Army which now understood that no help was to come in the forseeable future.

English: Following the success of the latest Republican offensive, the Nationalist Army was in dire straits. Almost three years since the start of military coup, and victory seemed further than ever. All attempts to rectify the situation, even the huge and bloody Levante Offensive, had failed to yield any meaningful gains. Even worse news, however, came not from the battlefiled, but from the foreign capitals. With the end of Czechoslovakia and the British guarantee to Poland, a big European war seemed closer than in 1914. If it were to happen, the isolated Nationalists would likely face the full wrath of the French Army and the British Navy. Franco's only hope was to win the war in Spain before such a conflict breaks out, but now this hope was completely dashed. This had a serious effect of the morale of the Nationalist Army which now understood that their prospects of victory were razor thin.

English: Organized by the Comintern and funded by the Soviet Union, international leftist volunteers began to arrive in Spain in serious numbers in the fall of 1936 and continued into early 1937. The Comintern then used these volunteers to form International Brigades, provide them with basic training and quickly sent them to the front lines. Despite the name, however, the percentage of the actual foreigners in each one of the Interbrigades was typically low, often less than 20 percent, the rest were locally conscripted Spanish. Another problem was low attritional endurance of the foreigners - they generally came expecting a short conflict, and when victory failed to quickly materialize, they became weary and demoralized, and the flow of new volunteers abruptly ended.

English: The Instrument of Accession was a legal document first introduced by the Government of India Act 1935 to enable each of the rulers of the princely states under British paramountcy to join one of the new dominions of India or Pakistan created by the Partition of British India. When India and Pakistan became independent, it would be a matter for each ruler of a state to decide whether they would accede to India, to Pakistan, or to declare full sovereignty. As the latter option was typically unacceptable to both Delhi and Islamabad, rulers considering independence were often pressured into signing 'standstill agreements', which provided for the existing administrative arrangements between the signatory dominion (India or Pakistan) and the princely state to continue unaltered for a specified period of usually up to 12 months, until new arrangements could be agreed upon.

As the latter option was typically unacceptable to both Delhi and Islamabad, rulers considering independence were often pressured into signing 'standstill agreements', which provided for the existing administrative arrangements between the signatory dominion (India or Pakistan) and the princely state to continue unaltered for a specified period of usually up to 12 months, until new arrangements could be agreed upon.

The UN Commission, which was initially created on India's own initiative, now passed an unanimous resolution demanding an immediate ceasefire. English: Since the Irish War of Independence and the partition of the island, Ireland's relations with London were governed by the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921. This treaty, however, was very contraversial and unpopular in Ireland, particularly among the supporters of Eamon de Valera, who led a party named 'Soldiers of Destiny' or 'Fianna Fail'. He advocated a complete break with Britiain and establishment of a fully-sovereign Irish Republic. By 1927, Fianna Fail began to make rapid political gains, and the treaty started to slowly become undone. In 1932, Fianna Fail secured majority in the Irish elections, and the Anglo-Irish relations quickly deteriorated, with UK imposing economic sanctions against Irish exports and De Valera responding in kind with levies on British imports. In late 1937, Ireland unilaterally abolished the office of the Governor-General representing the British monarch, and passed a new Constitution, officially ending the Irish Free State and establishing the Irish Republic. In 1938, UK and Ireland concluded a treaty settling their main outstanding disputes, and the last British bases known as 'Treaty Ports' were withdrawn from Ireland in the same year.

English: Diplomatic relations between Poland and USSR were re-established in 1941 after the German invasion of the Soviet Union, when the British government allied itself with the Soviet Union and pressured the Polish government in exile to act accordingly. Consequently, the USSR and Poland signed the Sikorski–Mayski agreement, whereby Joseph Stalin agreed to abrogate the Poland-related aspects of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact. As an amnesty for Polish citizens in the Soviet Union was negotiated, tens of thousands of Polish prisoners of war held in Soviet camps, as well as hundreds of thousands of Polish citizens who had been deported to the USSR, were released. From them the USSR began forming a new Polish Army based in Buzuluk (later in Tashkent), with the aim of fighting against the Germans alongside the Soviet Red Army. The Army was led by General Wladyslaw Anders, chosen by the exiled Polish government.

English: While the formation of the Polish Army in the East proceeded mostly as planned, Anders and the rest of the Polish leadership would ultimately refuse to fight under Soviet leadership. Beria reported to Stalin anti-Soviet sentiments among the Polish soldiers, while the generals expressed their strong preference to leave the USSR and fight elsewhere. Repeated Soviet attempts to get the Polish divisions to assist the Soviet army in the pivotal battles of the Eastern Front were resolutely declined by the Polish leadership, and Stalin developed paranoia about a possible Polish rebellion in the middle of Siberia, akin to the Chechoslovak rebellion which sparked the bloody Russian Civil War 25 years prior. Ultimately, the Soviet leadership came to the conclusion that its funding of the Polish army on its territory was a dangerous waste of limited resources, and began to stiffle the aid, much to the dismay of the Polish generals. Finally, by agreement with the British goverment, the Polish army was evacuated from USSR through Iran to Africa, and later fought together with the British and Americans in Italy and in France. Meanwhile, for Moscow, its support for the Army of Anders was not entirely a waste. Aside from helping a common Allied cause of defeating the Axis, the USSR was also able to rid itself from the most troublesome Polish elements, to normalize relations with the average working Poles by presenting itself as a friend to Poland rather than a foe, and finally allowed for the creation of a brand new Polish army, one that would actually fight alongside the USSR.

English: Following Italy's entry into World War II in June 1940, Italian forces invaded Greece and Egypt from their colonies in Albania and Libya. By the Spring of 1941 both these invasions had been defeated, but the threat of intervention by Germany persuaded Winston Churchill to commit British forces to the defence of the Greek mainland. Churchill thought it politically unacceptable not to support Britain's only effective ally in Europe under threat, especially after the Allies had already failed to come to the defense of Poland a year prior. In addition, the use of Greek airfields could put the Romanian oilfields at Ploiesti, vital to Germany's war effort, within reach of Allied bombers. Should we choose to assist Greece, we will be expected to deliver at least 6 British or Commonwealth divisions in mainland Greece within the next month. Note: Only troops from the UK, Canada, South Africa, India proper, Australia, New Zealand, as well as Poland are counted for this purpose.

English: Maurice Duplessis, the leader of the Union Nationale, embodied a conservative, Catholic nationalism that fiercely defended Quebec's autonomy against perceived Anglo-Canadian encroachment. His political rise in the 1930s capitalized on economic discontent and French-Canadian fears of assimilation, blending traditionalist values with inflammatory anti-establishment rhetoric. Duplessis was ousted in the 1939 election amid backlash over his handling of wartime preparations and accusations of corruption. For a while, his ouster significantly reduced apparent tensions between French and Anglo-Canadians, although he continued to exercise significant influence as the leader of the opposition and disagreements continued to simmer beneath the surface, so much so that the government was unable to enact overseas conscription all the way until 1944. The same year Duplessis returned to power, beginning his long-lasting and polarizing 'Great Darkness' regime, marked by even stronger nationalist policies and resistance to federal authority.

English: Upon the start of World War II in 1939, the Portuguese Government announced that the 600-year-old Anglo-Portuguese Alliance remained intact, but that since the British did not seek Portuguese assistance, Portugal was free to remain neutral in the war and would do so. In an aide-memoire of 5 September 1939, the British Government confirmed the understanding. However, the strategic location of the Azores made them highly valuable for both the Allies and the Axis powers. Control over the islands could facilitate transatlantic supply routes, sumbarine or anti-submarine operations, and reconnaissance missions. Each side made plans to invade the Azores, and the Allies began to put pressure on Portugal to grant them access to the islands. The Allies considered seizing the islands by force if the negotiations failed, however, ultimately seeing that the war was clearly progressing in the Allies favor, Portigal signed an agreement giving the Allies access to the Azores.

English: In May, in the Third Washington Conference, code-named Trident, the conferees agreed that the occupation of the Azores was essential to the conduct of the anti-U-boat campaign, extending Allied air cover for convoys and increasing harassing activities against U-boats. Delighted with the American stance Churchill cabled home with instructions: Portugal should be informed that if it refused to hand over the base, the Azores would be occupied. Luckily for both sides, the use of force turned out to be unnecessary. When the British requested military base facilities in the Azores, invoking the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance, Salazar responded favorably and quickly: Portugal allowed these bases, letting the British use the Azorean ports of Horta (on the island of Faial) and Ponta Delgada (on the island of Sao Miguel), and the airfields of Lajes Field (on Terceira Island) and Santana Field (on Sao Miguel Island).

English: Upon the outbreak of war in Europe, Greece declared its strict neutrality, hoping to avoid the devastation of another great conflict. Britain, bound by long-standing ties of friendship and aware of Greece's strategic position astride the eastern Mediterranean, initially respected this stance. Yet as Axis submarines and bombers extended their reach across the region, the importance of Crete and the Aegean became impossible for the Allies to ignore. From Crete, aircraft could protect convoys bound for Egypt and the Suez Canal, while naval bases there would secure the sea lanes between Gibraltar and the Levant. In private communications, London urged Athens to permit the use of Greek ports and airfields 'for defensive purposes.' When diplomatic appeals met hesitation, the British government began to consider unilateral action, fearing that Axis forces might seize the island first. Greece now faced a grave choice - to preserve neutrality at all costs, or risk becoming a battlefield between the great powers.

English: As the struggle for control of the Mediterranean intensified, Allied planners concluded that securing bases in the eastern Aegean was vital for sustaining operations in North Africa and safeguarding the sea routes to the Suez Canal. At the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting in Washington, British and American representatives agreed that the occupation of Crete would greatly extend Allied air and naval coverage, closing the dangerous gap through which Axis submarines preyed upon convoys bound for Egypt. Churchill, buoyed by the U.S. position, cabled London with instructions that Greece must be persuaded, or compelled, to grant access to the island's facilities. English: In the age of rising nation-states, our country is somewhat of an exception. Instead of representing a single ethnicity, our country is a union of two or more ethnic groups, theoretically equal, and united partly by blood and history, but more so by a set of common traditions and beliefs. Our country is an idea - which aims to create a sense of common destiny among believers. This is both our strength, and our weakness. Managing the interests of different ethnic groups, often with different pasts, grievances, and interests - is a rather challenging endeavor. It puts strain on our politics, on our social cohesion, and even on our economy. To make matters worse, there are certain groups which don't feel represented at all, and all attempts to reconcile their interests with those of our wider national community are so far proving to be elusive. The issue of our relations with these groups presents an additional destabilizing factor which we have yet to tackle.

English: The Roosevelt administration is deeply opposed to any potential German victory in Europe and likewise Japanese victory in China, and considers them both to be antithetical to the US security and economic needs. From his perspective, the United States has a vital interest in preserving the balance of power and preventing the emergence of hegemonic rivals in both Europe and Asia. The best possible outcome is therefore for Germany and Japan to get bogged down in endless wars with minimal direct US involvement. However, if either Germany or Japan get too close to victory - the US would have no choice but to intervene directly. But this will not be easy. Much of the American population consists of ethnic Germans, Italians, and Irish - many of whom are loath to see yet another US intervention on the side of the British, especially given that the last such intervention did not appear to bring them much tangible benefit. Intervention in the war is opposed by many veterans of WW1, right-wingers, religious groups and pacifist organizations, industrialists profiting from trade with the Axis powers, as well as ordinary citizens impoverished by the Great Depression and deeply worried about the economic cost of another war. We should expect any intervention on the side of the Allies to be rather unpopular. However, if we can provoke the Axis into a direct attack on our forces - then we can blunt the impact of popular opposition considerably. On the other hand, overly belligerent behavior by the Allies (mainly UK and USSR) will make intervention on their side more difficult still.

The best possible outcome is therefore for Germany and Japan to get bogged down in endless wars with minimal direct US involvement. However, if either Germany or Japan get too close to victory - the US would have no choice but to intervene directly. But this will not be easy. Much of the American population consists of ethnic Germans, Italians, and Irish - many of whom are loath to see yet another US intervention on the side of the British, especially given that the last such intervention did not appear to bring them much tangible benefit. Intervention in the war is opposed by many veterans of WW1, right-wingers, religious groups and pacifist organizations, industrialists profiting from trade with the Axis powers, as well as ordinary citizens impoverished by the Great Depression and deeply worried about the economic cost of another war. We should expect any intervention on the side of the Allies to be rather unpopular. However, if we can provoke the Axis into a direct attack on our forces - then we can blunt the impact of popular opposition considerably. On the other hand, overly belligerent behavior by the Allies (mainly UK and USSR) will make intervention on their side more difficult still.

English: When the full scale Sino-Japanese war broke out, the U.S. initially found itself arming both sides at the same time. However, in light of the Chinese losing territory and Japanese committing atrocities, the US sympathy quickly tilted towards the Chinese side and the administration started to provide limited aid to China, such as in the form of the Pittman Act, which enabled the United States Treasury to exchange Chinese silver dollars for American gold. This exchange provided the Chinese government with greater access to foreign credit which allowed the Chinese army to purchase critical military supplies.

The withdrawal from the treaty enabled the administration to start placing significantly heavier sanctions on Japan, and six months later the US placed restrictions on the export of strategic materials like machine tools and chemicals that could be used for military purposes. Meanwhile, more clandestine aid was delivered to China through intermediaries.

Meanwhile, more clandestine aid was delivered to China through intermediaries.

English: Following continued Japanese advances in China and North Indochina, the U.S. extended a $25 million loan to China for the purchase of military supplies. A few months later, the Lend-Lease Act was passed by the U.S. Congress, allowing the U.S. to supply military aid to foreign nations, including China, without immediate payment, beginning the direct shipments of aircraft, vehicles, and other military supplies. The first American Volunteer Group (AVG), known as the Flying Tigers, was formed under the command of Claire Lee Chennault. This group of American pilots assists the Chinese Air Force in combat against Japanese forces. Meanwhile, the U.S. also froze Japanese assets, restricting Japan's access to funds needed for international trade.

In the next couple of months, the embargo was extended to include all exports of gasoline and lubricants as well as the exports of various strategic materials, including precious metals and industrial machinery. United Kingdom and Netherlands joined the embargo. Following the embargo, the IJN headquarters informed Emperor Hirohito that its reserve bunker oil would be exhausted within two years if a new source was not found.

English: Following the outbreak of war in Europe, Roosevelt finally managed to convince Congress to sign a new 'Neutrality Act' of 1939. This act, despite its name, allowed for arms trade with belligerent nations on a cash-and-carry basis, thus in effect ending the neutral arms embargo. Furthermore, the National Munitions Control Board (which had been created by the 1935 Neutrality Act) was charged with issuing licenses for all arms imports and exports. Arms trade without a license became a federal crime. This allowed the administration to make sure that arms trade went specifically to support Britain and France, and not Germany.

English: Following the fall of France, the US sent a proposal to London for rent-free American lease of bases on Trinidad, Bermuda, and Newfoundland. The British, although desperate for help, initially refused this brazen offer.  But as the Battle of Britain intensified, Churchill managed to work out a deal with Roosevelt for an expanded list of US bases in exchange for destroyers to help deal with the German submarine threat, and Roosevelt pushed through the agreement despite opposition from Congress. The US received rights to about 23 different bases in the Western hemisphere, in return for the shipment of 50 destroyers to the UK. The destroyers were very old and in bad condition, and the resulting deal was so one-sided that Churchill's aide John Colville compared it to the USSR's proposals to Finland. Effectively, Britain ceded control over some of its Empire for the duration of the war to the US for safekeeping. Still, it was felt that this agreement was a necessary step to keep Britain fighting and to unlock further assistance from the United States down the road. To sweeten the deal, Roosevelt declared as 'surplus' many millions of rounds of US ammunition and obsolescent small arms and authorized their shipment to Britain.

But as the Battle of Britain intensified, Churchill managed to work out a deal with Roosevelt for an expanded list of US bases in exchange for destroyers to help deal with the German submarine threat, and Roosevelt pushed through the agreement despite opposition from Congress. The US received rights to about 23 different bases in the Western hemisphere, in return for the shipment of 50 destroyers to the UK. The destroyers were very old and in bad condition, and the resulting deal was so one-sided that Churchill's aide John Colville compared it to the USSR's proposals to Finland. Effectively, Britain ceded control over some of its Empire for the duration of the war to the US for safekeeping. Still, it was felt that this agreement was a necessary step to keep Britain fighting and to unlock further assistance from the United States down the road. To sweeten the deal, Roosevelt declared as 'surplus' many millions of rounds of US ammunition and obsolescent small arms and authorized their shipment to Britain.

English: Since 1939, Britain had been paying for its materiel with gold as part of the 'cash and carry' program, as required by the U.S. Neutrality Acts of the 1930s, but by 1941 it had liquidated a large part of its overseas holdings and its gold reserves were becoming depleted in paying for materiel from the United States. As the US was just beginning to mobilize for war, Great Britain was running out of liquid currency and asked not to be forced to sell off British assets. In March 1941, Congress passed the Lend-Lease act, allowing for the delivery of military supplies to belligerent nations at no cost, to be used until returned or destroyed. Meanwhile, the U.S. froze German and Axis assets in American banks as part of broader financial controls designed to limit access to American resources, and a month later it placed an embargo on the export of oil and other strategic materials to Germany. Effectively, the decision to enter the war was made.

English: Six months after the passage of the lend-lease act, the USS Greer, an American destroyer, was tracking a German U-boat, U-652, off the coast of Iceland. The Greer and the U-boat exchanged fire, with the U-boat firing torpedoes that missed the destroyer. President Franklin D. Roosevelt used the incident to justify a 'shoot-on-sight' policy, ordering the U.S. Navy to attack any Axis warships encountered in the North Atlantic. Effectively, this meant the beginning of an undeclared war against Germany. One month later, destroyer USS Reuben James was sunk by a German submarine while escorting a convoy to the UK. The attack resulted in the loss of 115 American sailors. Following this, Congress amended the Neutrality Act to allow the arming of American merchant ships and permit them to enter combat zones, further aligning U.S. policy with the needs of the Allies. However, large scale operations against Germany were still out of the question until Congress officially declared war. If we were to ally with UK or deploy our troops to Europe, for example, the Congress will be very upset.

They claim that the administration is unnecessarily dragging the US into a foreign war without a pressing need or vital US interests at stake in the matter. Furthermore, by failing to coordinate its policy with the Congress or take its opinion into account, the administration is acting in an increasingly dictatorial manner. Nobody wants a new Ceasar, or worse, a new Furher. During the Senate hearings today, the subject of foreign troop deployments and diplomatic alliances was raised. We either need to urgently withdraw our troops from overseas and abrogate the illegal foreign entanglements, convince the Congress to actually declare war, or prepare to face intense Congressional opposition and possibly impeachment. What shall we tell the Senate?

Deliveres were made via the Arctic Convoys, the Persian Corridor, and the Pacific Route. The Arctic route was the shortest and most direct route for lend-lease aid to the USSR, though it was also the most dangerous as it involved sailing past German-occupied Norway. Some 3,964,000 tons of goods were shipped by the Arctic route

English: Following the full scale invasion of China by Japan, the Soviet and Chinese relations rapidly improved. In August, China and USSR signed a treaty of non-aggression, and in September, the CCP was officially legalized in China. The 'Chinese Soviet Republic' was abolished, and the army of CCP was transformed into units of the National Revolutionary Army of China primarily under the names 'New 4th Army' and '8th Route Army'. Communists agreed to accept the leadership of Chiang Kai-Shek, and in return they began to receive financial support from the central government. In this atmosphere, the Soviet Union began 'Operation Z' - a program of massive military assistance to China, with the aim of preventing a Japanese victory at all costs.

English: The Soviet Volunteer Group was the volunteer part of the Soviet Air Forces sent to support the Republic of China during the Second Sino-Japanese War. The Soviet pilots and technicians arrived as private citizens and initially wore civilian clothing, the mission remaining a secret even from their closest relatives. They were instructed to avoid using the term comrade, and in the event of their capture they were to claim that they were former members of the White movement permanently residing in China. Prior to each mission, the pilots changed into Chinese uniforms, whilst their planes were marked with Chinese Air Force insignia. Over 1,200 aircraft had been sent to China by the end of 1941.

English: Our current western border was drawn in the aftermath of the Polish-Soviet war which was fought 15 years earlier and ended inconlusively. It left much of our former territory under Polish rule, including many of our Ukrainian and Belorussian brothers. Even more importantly, it left the security of our country in a somewhat fragile state, with the Eastern polish border only 500km away from Moscow and even closer to Leningrad. If Germany were to take all of Poland, this would be an enormous security problem. While the pact we signed with Germany promises Eastern Poland to us, it is abundantly apparent that agreements reached with Hitler mean nothing unless they are backed up by force. For this reason alone, we must act, and act quickly.

English: The news of the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact was met with utter shock and surprise by reporters worldwide, most being aware only of the British–French–Soviet negotiations that had taken place for months. Even fewer had guessed that in addition to stipulations of non-aggression, the treaty included a secret protocol dividing several eastern European countries between the parties. Not long after Germany attacked Poland, the Soviet troops moved in from the East and also engaged the Polish army. As allies of Poland and guarantors of Polish independence, we now have a difficult decision to make.

English: As it turns out, Ribbentrop's mission in Moscow was just a stalling tactic rather than a genuine attempt to reach an agreement. Instead, Germany called our bluff and attacked Poland without our blessing. No matter what we do now, it clear that the clash against Germany is both inevitable and imminent. If we let them take Poland, we will be next, there is no question about it. The cursed British have gotten exactly what they wanted - Germany and USSR will fight each other while they watch from across the channel and make money. Even so, we have no choice in the matter any more, we urgently need their help. We can sign a formal treaty promising to respect Poland's territorial integrity, then we will be allowed to enter Poland and save the Polish army from destruction. Perhaps we can still subjugate Poland later...

English: Our population is growing increasingly restless by the continuing war against Finland. Most people have been expecting a rapid and nearly bloodless campaign against a small and sparsely populated neighboring state. They were unpleasantly surprised to find their country entangled in a long and bloody struggle with no apparent end in sight. These treasonous attitudes are amplified by the fact that most Soviet people don't understand this war and don't feel existentially threatened by Finland, so there is a growing lack of enthusiasm for continuing sacrifices which have to be made. This dissatifaction is rapidly seeping into the Party committees and the Soviet Ispolkoms, which increases the risk to our hard-won unity at a time when we need to maintain maximum cohesion and preparedness against grave dangers. Meanwhile at the Politburo, comrades most loyal to Stalin are advising to find a way to end this war quickly as it is proving to be a dangerous drain on the Soviet treasury and manpower. If we are not able to achieve our primary goals, they suggest offering a face-saving compromise to Finland as a way out.

English: The initial Soviet invasion led to a great outburst of patriotism and unification of the Finnish society, previously plagued by deep fissures. The resounding Finnish victories of the early war against thoroughly unprepared Soviet troops, the outpouring of international support and promises of imminent Anglo-French intervention greatly boosted the morale of the Finnish troops. But as the conflict appeared to settle into a war of attrition and casualties began to mount, and as the promised Anglo-French intervention failed to materialize, the Finns had to grapple with the harsh reality of the conflict, and morale started to falter once again. Without direct Western intervention, the Finns simply had no answer to the massive preponderance of Soviet artillery and air power, and its seemingly infinite manpower.

English: With the USSR distracted by its war with Germany, Sheng approached the Chinese government in July 1942 for reconciliation talks. The final months of 1942 saw the most turbulent period in Xinjiang-Soviet relations. In October 1942 Sheng demanded from the Soviet General Consul that all Soviet technical and military personnel be withdrawn from Xinjiang within three months. Despite Sheng's ultimatum, only in March–April 1943 did the Soviets notify Sheng and the Chinese government of their withdrawal. The Kuomintang representatives and personnel filled the void. In June 1943, four divisions of the NRA New 2nd Army were transferred to Xinjiang from Gansu. In October 1943, the Kuomintang effectively removed Soviet influence from Xinjiang. With the Soviets gone, in September Sheng ordered the arrest and execution of the CCP cadres.

Among them was Mao Zemin, Mao Zedong's younger brother, who was among eighty-eight conspirators involved in the Soviet plot to overthrow Sheng.

English: At the beginning of Operation Barbarossa, Adolf Hitler reluctantly agreed to allow recruitment of Soviet citizens in the Rear Areas of the Wehrmacht. Most were recruited from the POW camps and already had both training and experience, although it was considered subpar by German standards and their reliability was often questionable. In a short period of time, many such volunteers were moved to frontline combat units and fought side by side with the German Army. To avoid possible concentrated resistance, these ethnic formations known to the Germans as 'Osttruppen' and 'Hiwis' tended to be split among a mosaic of different units both under the Wehrmacht and under Waffen SS. Towards the end of the war, in attempt to boost non-German recruitment as well as morale of existing Eastern troops, Berlin authorized to begin consolidating ethnic units into larger formations with clear political and ethnic orientations such as the Russian Liberation Army and Ukrainian Liberation Army, both of which, however, still performed rather poorly in combat.

English: Tuvan integration with USSR intensified during the war. The written language was changed to Cyrillic, the flag and emblem were changed to the same style as various Soviet regions, and virtually all remaining opposition to Stalinist policy was eradicated. The Mongolian designs on the territory held by Tuva also intisified the desire of the Tuvan elites to integrate into the USSR as a way to ensure security. Finally, under the rule of General Secretary Salchak Toka and his wife, Head of State Khertek Anchimaa-Toka, Tuva became part of the USSR and RSFSR.

English: Following the defeat in Winter War, much of the Finnish population favored the government's policy of pursuing the reconquest of the territory ceded to the Soviet Union. However, the Finns were simultaneously weary of joining a clearly offensive war against the Soviet Union on the German side without a clear cause, as the continued war would inevitably put significant strain on Finland's modest economy and demography, and even more so, because joining this war would put Finland firmly in the German camp and therefore make it an enemy of Great Britain and other Allied powers. In attempt to alleviate those fears, the Finnish Army deliberately abstained from joining the German offensive operations for the first couple of weeks of the war, effectively allowing the USSR to make the first move. Only after the Soviets had repeatedly bombed Finnish cities and caused significant civilian losses, and as the German invasion clearly showed signs of early success, the Finns decided to declare war and commence offensive operations of their own.

English: Between 1921 and 1926, the Soviet economy rapidly recovered from the chaos of WW1 and Civil War under the program called 'New Economic Policy' (NEP), which combined elements of socialist and capitalist modes of production. By mid 1920s, however, the room for recovery had largely been exhausted, and in 1927, a series of economic crises and a fear of a looming war with the West forced the Soviet leadership to reconsider the continued utility of NEP. There were two competing schools of thought - one argued that the Soviet Union could not afford to slow down its economic growth, especially while surrounded by potentially hostile capitalist powers, and that NEP should be abandoned in favor of a program of rapid forced industrialization by means of nationalisation, collectivisation, and ambitious five-year development goals. Consumer goods spending was to be artificially slashed and capital redirected towards the growth of heavy industry. Any resulting dissent and dissatisfaction would have to be ruthlessly crushed. The other school of thought argued that NEP should be preserved, but the lower rates of growth were natural and expected. They warned that forced industrialization could lead to food shortages, inflation, and peasant uprisings. The debates in the VKP(b) over this subject became really heated, with Joseph Stalin initially backing the supporters of the NEP while Leon Trotsky and his allies advocated for five-year plans. But by 1928, with Trotsky defeated and exiled, Stalin himself had changed his mind on the subject and decided to support forced industrialization as well. In a speech before the 15th Congress of VKP(b), Stalin warned that without an end to economic backwardness 'the advanced countries...will crush us.' Thus, the VKP(b) approved the First Five-Year Plan, which served as the blueprint for future Soviet economic development for many decades.

English: The First Five-Year Plan (1928-1933) led to mixed results. Areas like capital goods increased 158\%, consumer goods increased by 87\%, and total industrial output increased by 118\%. Yet, these successes were still far below the goals initially outlined by the planning committee, and the cost to the Soviet people - particularly the peasantry, was very severe. The plan ended with a massive famine of 1932-1933 which claimed the lives of between 3.3 and 7.5 million people, and led to a serious slump in the the overall production, particularly in the agricultural sector. Despite this, the achievements of the first plan laid the foundation for the much more successuful Second Five-Year Plan (1933-1937), which saw an explosive growth in Soviet economic output. While much of the capitalist world was suffering from the Great Depression, the USSR saw overall GNP growth averages of 10\% to 12\% per year. But these achievements also did not come for free, they were only made possible by a forced labor system and an increasingly repressive state apparatus, which led directly to the massive purges of 1937-1938. Finally, the Third Five-Year Plan was adopted in the midst of rising tensions in Europe and focused mostly on the devlopment of war industries and a growth in defense spending.
